Free to read and share. You may print, copy and share this book for personal use and for non-commercial teaching, as long as you credit “Spread Love & Acceptance, spreadloveandacceptance.com” and don’t change it or sell it.

Not therapy. This book is general education about people and relationships. It is not a diagnosis, treatment or a replacement for help from a doctor, counsellor or other trained professional, and it can’t know your situation.

If you are not safe. If you feel afraid of someone you live with, or someone controls your money, phone or movements, that is not a problem to fix with a worksheet. spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety lists free, private help. If you are in danger now, call your local emergency number.

The examples are made up. The people in the scenes and examples are invented, built from common patterns. None of them is a real person or a testimonial.

If you need help now

If you might act on thoughts of ending your life, or someone is in danger right now, call your local emergency number: 999 in the UK, 112 or 999 in Ireland, 911 in the US and Canada, 000 in Australia, 111 in New Zealand.

If you are struggling, or worried about someone else, you can talk to a trained person now. These lines are free, private and open day and night. You don’t have to be sure it is a crisis to call or text.

Where you areCall or text
United StatesCall or text 988 (the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline), or chat at 988lifeline.org. You can also text HOME to 741741 (Crisis Text Line).
United KingdomCall Samaritans free on 116 123. Or text SHOUT to 85258 (Shout, a free text line).
IrelandCall Samaritans free on 116 123.
CanadaCall or text 9-8-8 (the Suicide Crisis Helpline), in English or French.
AustraliaCall Lifeline on 13 11 14, or text 0477 13 11 14.
New ZealandCall or text 1737 (Need to talk?).
Anywhere elsefindahelpline.com lists free helplines in many countries, by phone, text and chat.

For children and young people

UKChildline, 0800 1111 (free, for anyone under 19)
IrelandChildline, 1800 66 66 66 (free, for anyone up to 18)
CanadaKids Help Phone, 1-800-668-6868, or text CONNECT to 686868
AustraliaKids Helpline, 1800 55 1800 (ages 5 to 25)
New ZealandYouthline, 0800 376 633, or text 234
US988 is for every age.

If you’re worried about someone

Ask them plainly: “Are you thinking about ending your life?” Studies have found that asking does not put the idea in someone’s head, and talking about it may even ease it. Listen, stay with them if you can, and call or text one of the lines above together. Part Three, Chapter 12, page 170 says more about helping someone in a crisis, and Chapter 16, page 236 about worry, low mood and when to get help.

This book is general education, not a crisis service. The website’s tools keep what you type on your own device, so nobody there can see it or reply to it. The numbers were checked in October 2026. Numbers can change; findahelpline.com keeps an up-to-date list.

How to use this book

This is a book about seeing what is really going on, in yourself and between people, without blaming anyone, and then changing one small thing. This copy holds 17 chapters in one part, in the short version. There is no wrong way in.

The parts

  • Part Three: Understanding people. How feelings, stress, trust, change, grief, groups and love work, for anyone, in any kind of relationship.

Two sizes of every chapter

Every chapter comes in a short version (about 10 to 15 minutes) and a full version with the research, more examples and more to try. This is the short version. The full version is free at spreadloveandacceptance.com/book.

Read in order, or by need

Read it front to back like any book, or start with the chapter that fits what is going on. Each chapter ends with What to remember, This connects to (the chapters that explain it or put it to use, with page numbers) and Put it to use, with codes you can scan for the matching tool.

In every chapter

  • A short scene: a made-up moment from everyday life.
  • Words you could use: sentences to say out loud.
  • Try this: one small thing to do this week.
  • Common mix-ups: easy mistakes, and what is closer to true.

The site, the program and Professor Puddles

The book has a free website with the workpapers (pages you fill in) and tools (helpers you use) that the chapters mention; the next page explains both. Nothing you type there leaves your device, and there is no account. The six-week program (spreadloveandacceptance.com/prog-01) puts Part Two to work a week at a time, and the self path does the same for Part One. Professor Puddles, the site’s friendly guide, answers questions about the book’s ideas.

Go gently

Some chapters touch hard things: grief, shame, anger, worry, trauma. Skip anything that isn’t right for today. Nothing here is a test, and nothing needs to be done all at once.

Workpapers, tools and three friends

Workpaper WP-03 Workpapers: pages you fill in

A workpaper is a page you fill in, on your own or together: a one-week log, a list of who owns which job, a short check. Each one has a number, like WP-03, and it is always called a workpaper, for example “Workpaper WP-03: One owner per job”. The blank workpapers are also at the back of this book, one page each, to copy.

Tool Tools: helpers you use on the site

A tool is an interactive helper on the website: a quiz, a calm-down timer, a card maker, or the Chat analyzer that reads a message with you. You use it and it gives you something back. It is always called a tool, for example “Tool: Chat analyzer”.

The book keeps the two apart: a workpaper and a tool never share a list. Both are free, need no account, and what you type stays on your device.

Three friends who give hints

  • Professor Puddles, the site’s cheerful raindrop professor, gives most of the hints: a thought to take with you, and the workpaper or tool that fits.
  • Tidbit, the quick, curious pup with the big smile and the collar, bounds in now and then with a playful tip.
  • Sugarfoot, the steady, gentle pup with the long soft ears and the best hugs, turns up with a calm, slow tip.

They keep to the lighter pages. Where a chapter talks about crisis, deep grief or being hurt, the pages stay quiet and plain.

Part Three · Chapter 1

How feelings work: signals, the body, and naming what you feel

What feelings are for, where they start, and why putting a name to one can make it easier to carry, whether you’re on your own, at home, with friends or at work.

In this chapter

  1. A feeling is a signal, not a verdict
  2. Feelings start in the body
  3. Naming a feeling helps you hold it
  4. More words, better tools
  5. Feelings come in layers
  6. Feelings rise and pass like waves
  7. Feelings spread between people
  8. If you weren’t brought up to talk about feelings
  9. Feeling it isn’t the same as doing it
  10. In everyday life
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. When to get more help
  14. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  15. More for your situation

In short

  • A feeling is a signal that something matters to you. It doesn’t tell you what to do about it.
  • Feelings start in the body. A tight chest or a hot face often arrives before the word for it.
  • Naming helps. “I feel let down” is easier to hold than a big, nameless rush.
  • You can let a feeling be there and still choose what you do next.

Thursday, 4:50pm

A message from your manager: “Have you got a minute tomorrow?” No full stop, no smiley, nothing else. Your stomach drops. By the time you get home you’ve snapped at the cat, skipped dinner and replayed every mistake of the last month, including one from March that nobody else remembers, although nobody has said anything bad at all.

Feelings sit underneath almost everything else in this book, from how we talk to how we handle stress. This chapter looks at how they work first, and then at what to do with them. Two tools elsewhere lean on it. My weather today and the daily check-in (Part One, Now, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/self-2-now; Part Two, Chapter I, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-1) ask for one word about how you are, because naming a feeling turns its volume down a little and a daily word catches feelings while they’re small. And Say it so it lands (Part Two, Chapter IV, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-4) asks you to describe a feeling, because “I felt let down” is a great deal easier to hear than “you never care.”

  1. A feeling is a signal, not a verdict.

    Feelings are fast messages about what matters to you. Fear warns that something might be dangerous. Anger says something seems unfair, or in your way. Sadness says you’ve lost something that mattered. A signal is worth listening to, but it can be wrong about the details, the way a smoke alarm goes off for burnt toast with exactly the same urgency it would use for a fire.

    Say you feel jealous when a friend makes a new close friend. The jealousy proves nothing about you, and nothing about whether your friend is drifting off. What it shows is how much the friendship matters to you, which is worth knowing, and possibly worth telling her.

    Things to tell yourself “This feeling is telling me something matters. What is it?” “Is this the fire, or the toast?”

    Dig deeper: what feelings are for

  2. Feelings start in the body.

    Often your body reacts before your mind has a word for what’s going on: a racing heart, a hot face, a heavy chest, a knot in the stomach. Then the brain tries to make sense of the signal, and it guesses. That’s why being hungry or tired or in pain can feel so like being upset.

    A teenager comes home furious with his mum over very little, something about a towel. After a cheese sandwich and twenty minutes on the sofa with the dog, most of the fury has gone, and he admits, with some reluctance, that he skipped lunch. A few times today, stop and ask what your body feels like right now. Is there hunger in it, or cold, or a sore back?

    Dig deeper: the body and the brain’s best guess

  3. Naming a feeling helps you hold it.

    Putting a feeling into words can turn its volume down. In brain-scan research by Lieberman and colleagues (2007), simply putting a name to a feeling (“I feel scared”) turned down the brain’s alarm response. A name gives a big, cloudy rush some edges, so you can see it and talk about it and decide what to do.

    Two housemates are tense all evening, passing each other in the hall without a word. Eventually one says, “I think I’m embarrassed about the noise complaint, and I’ve been acting cross.” The other, who had spent two hours wondering what she’d done wrong, puts the kettle on.

    You could say “I think what I’m feeling is…” “I’m not sure what this is yet. Maybe worried?”

    Once a day, name one feeling, out loud or on paper. A guess like “something like sad” still counts.

    Dig deeper: why naming works

    Professor Puddles

    If the words won’t come, weather words often will. “Foggy” or “stormy” is a perfectly good place to start.

    Tool: My weather today spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks

  4. More words, better tools.

    “Bad” is a very blunt word. Disappointed is different from left out, and both are different from overwhelmed or ashamed; each points somewhere different and needs something different. A review by Kashdan, Barrett and McKnight (2015) found that people who can tell their feelings apart more finely tend to cope with them in healthier ways. You don’t need fancy words. A number works, and so does a colour.

    A dad tells his partner he feels bad about his mum, and they go round in circles for half an hour. Then he says, “Actually, I feel guilty that I haven’t been up to see her since Easter, and scared she’s getting worse,” and within ten minutes they’re looking at train times to Carlisle.

    Words you could use “On a scale of one to ten, I’m about a six.” “It’s less angry and more… let down.” “It feels heavy, like a grey day.”

    Dig deeper: finer words, finer tools

  5. Feelings come in layers.

    The feeling you show first isn’t always the one you felt first. Anger is very often a cover for hurt or fear, because anger feels stronger and safer to stand in. We also have feelings about our feelings, like being ashamed of being sad, and that second layer can sting more than the first.

    A grandmother is curt with her daughter on the phone after the half-term visit is cancelled for the second time. Under the curtness is hurt. Under the hurt, if she let herself look, is a quieter fear that she isn’t needed much any more. She doesn’t say any of that. She says “Fine, well, another time,” and then sits by the phone for a while. Next time you feel angry, ask yourself whether there’s hurt or worry underneath. You don’t have to tell anyone what you find.

    Dig deeper: first feelings and feelings about feelings

  6. Feelings rise and pass like waves.

    Most feelings, even big ones, rise and peak and settle if you don’t keep feeding them. Moods are another matter. A mood is more like weather, a background feeling that lasts hours or days and colours everything, often without you noticing it’s there.

    A woman who lives alone has a bad morning (the boiler, a bill, a dream about her ex) and by eleven has decided her whole life is going nowhere. By evening, after a walk along the canal and a long call with her sister, the same life looks ordinary and fairly okay, with a dentist’s appointment on Tuesday and a library book she wants to finish. Nothing in her life changed between eleven and seven. That’s a good reason to leave big decisions until the wave has passed: write the decision down and look at it again tomorrow.

    Things to tell yourself “This is a wave. It will peak and pass.” “Is this a feeling about now, or a mood colouring everything?”

    Dig deeper: waves and weather

  7. Feelings spread between people.

    We pick up each other’s feelings from a tense voice, a sigh or a door shut a bit too hard, usually without noticing. That’s part of how people bond. It also means stress can move round a home or a team like a cold in February.

    A team leader comes into the Monday meeting rushed and anxious, and within ten minutes the whole team feels behind on everything. The next week she stops outside the door for two slow breaths before she goes in, and the meeting finishes on time, which in that office counts as a minor miracle. You can care about someone’s feeling without catching all of it. Notice who you tend to catch feelings from, and before your next talk with them, give yourself one minute first.

    Things to tell yourself “Is this feeling mine, or did I pick it up?” “I can stay beside their storm without standing in the middle of it.”

    Dig deeper: how feelings spread

    Tidbit

    Good moods are catching too. If you’d like a small way to share one, there’s a tool for it.

    Tool: Stay close: one small idea spreadloveandacceptance.com/bonding

  8. If you weren’t brought up to talk about feelings.

    Lots of people grew up in homes, generations or cultures where feelings were kept private. “Don’t make a fuss.” “Big boys don’t cry.” “We don’t talk about that.” It’s especially common among men and older people, and in some cultures keeping your feelings to yourself is a sign of respect and strength.

    It isn’t a flaw, and it doesn’t mean you don’t feel. Many people who rarely put a feeling into words show it every single day by doing things: fixing the tap, driving someone to the hospital at two in the morning, simply turning up. Caring by doing is real caring. Words can be added slowly, a few at a time, if you want them.

    A retired builder whose wife has died has never talked about his feelings in his life. On the touchline at his grandson’s Saturday match, during a dull bit of the first half, he says to his son, “I wasn’t brought up to say this, but I miss her. Every morning.” His son puts a hand on his shoulder, and they watch the second half together without saying much else.

    Ways to say it “I wasn’t brought up to say this, but I miss her.” “I’m not good with words for this. It’s been a hard week.” “I don’t know what to call it. I just feel heavy.” “I’m not one for talking, but I wanted you to know I’m proud of you.”

    If one of those fits, you could say it once this week, to one person or just out loud in the car. A text counts, and so does writing it down.

    Dig deeper: when feelings weren’t talked about

  9. Feeling it isn’t the same as doing it.

    A feeling usually comes with an urge attached, to shout or run or hide or check or fix or text. You don’t choose the feeling. You have rather more say over the urge. Pushing a feeling down tends to bring it back stronger, and acting on every urge can hurt people, so the workable middle is to let the feeling be there and choose the action.

    A father hears glass go and looks out to see his son standing very still in the garden next to a football. He feels a hot rush of anger, says, “I’m too cross to talk right now. Let’s sort this out in ten minutes,” and goes to fetch the dustpan. If there’s one urge you often act on too fast, like the sharp text, make yourself a rule to wait ten minutes before you send it.

    Words to try “I’m feeling a lot right now. I’m going to take a minute before I answer.” “I want to reply when I’m calmer.”

    Dig deeper: feelings, urges and choices

Friday, 9:05am

The knot is there again, and this time you name it. You’re scared you’re in trouble. So you go and ask your manager straight away whether today’s chat is anything to worry about, and she looks genuinely surprised and says it’s about the summer rota. You go back to your desk and eat the breakfast you skipped, a slightly squashed banana.

In everyday life

If you live on your own, there’s nobody to notice how you are, so a one-word check-in with yourself each day matters more (see On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own). With a partner, “What are you feeling?” can sound like a test you might fail, while “Do you want to tell me, or shall I just sit with you?” is much easier to answer. Children learn feeling words from the adults around them, and hearing you say “I’m frustrated, so I’m taking a breath” teaches them more than any lesson would. At work, a short “I’m a bit flat today, and I’m not upset with anyone” can stop a whole team guessing. And if someone close to you shows care by doing, say by clearing the drive on a bad day, you can thank them for it in words. They may not know what to do with it the first time.

Common mix-ups

Some feelings are painful and some actions are harmful, but a feeling in itself isn’t bad; it’s information. Feeling stupid doesn’t make you stupid either. Treat a feeling as a signal to check before you obey it. Lots of people expect to be able to name what they feel straight away, and plenty can’t, some of them most days, which is why body words and numbers count as answers here. The last one is the most stubborn. We think a face tells us what someone feels, but faces are a poor guide. People show the same feeling in very different ways, and asking is both kinder and more accurate than guessing.

If you want to help someone else with this

Ask before you name it for them. “You’re angry” can land like a label, while “You seem upset. Am I reading that right?” leaves room for them to correct you. Then help the feeling make sense (“Of course you’re upset, that was a lot”), which helps more than advice and doesn’t mean you agree with everything they did. Offer a choice between ideas and just listening; a lot of people only want the second, and are relieved to be asked. Accept other ways of saying it, like a number, a text, a drawing or “I’m at a seven”. And settle yourself first. If their sadness makes you anxious, calm down before you go to them, so they don’t end up looking after your feelings as well as their own.

You could say “That sounds really hard.” “Do you want to talk, or would company help more?” “You don’t have to find the right word. A number is fine.”

When to get more help

Everyone has hard days and big feelings. It may be time to talk to a doctor, a counsellor or another trained professional if:

  • a low, numb, anxious or angry feeling stays most days for two weeks or more;
  • feelings are stopping you from sleeping, eating, working or seeing people;
  • you are using alcohol, drugs or other things to stop feeling;
  • you feel you can’t cope, or have thoughts of harming yourself. If that’s happening now, contact your local emergency number or a crisis line straight away. You deserve help today.

If you feel afraid of someone you live with or are close to, that fear is an important signal. It is not something to “manage” on your own. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private help.

This chapter is general education, not a diagnosis or therapy. It can’t know your situation.

Part Three · Chapter 2

Stress and the nervous system: the ladder, flooding, rest and recovery

What stress does to your body and your mind, why kind people say things they don’t mean when they’re flooded, and which kinds of rest actually put something back.

In this chapter

  1. Stress is your body getting ready
  2. Stress depends on what you have to meet it
  3. The ladder: three everyday states
  4. When you’re flooded, thinking goes offline
  5. Stress adds up, like a tank filling
  6. Settle the body first
  7. Rest isn’t one thing
  8. Sleep and stress feed each other
  9. Stress is easier to carry when it’s shared
  10. In everyday life
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. When to get more help
  14. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  15. More for your situation

Monday, 7:52am

The bus is late. One school shoe is missing, last seen under the sofa on Saturday, and your phone buzzes with a message from work that begins “Quick one”. Your partner calls from the hall, “Have you seen my keys?” and you hear yourself snap, “I’m not your secretary!”

A second later you wonder where that came from, because the keys were never the problem and you were running late before anyone said a word, before the shoe went missing, probably before you were even out of bed.

Feelings got their own chapter (Chapter 1, page 16). This one goes a layer down, to the nervous system that runs underneath them, and what it does when the pressure is on. Knowing how stress works won’t make a busy Monday any quieter. It does make your own reactions, and other people’s, a lot less mysterious.

It also explains why some of the tools elsewhere work at all. The stress tank in Part Two, Chapter III (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-3) asks you to check how full you are before you judge the moment, because stress piles up from small loads. The Calm-Down Kit in Part One, Now (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/self-2-now) settles the body before any words, and it asks you to name a time to come back, so a pause doesn’t look like walking out. The setup score in Part Two, Chapter II (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-2) counts stress as well as hours, since a split can look fair on paper and still leave one person running on empty.

  1. Stress is your body getting ready.

    Something needs dealing with, and your body gears up before you’ve decided anything. Heart faster, breath quicker, muscles tight, stress hormones up. That’s exactly what you want when a glass is sliding off the table. The trouble comes when the body stays geared up for hours and never gets the signal to stand down.

    Morag is a nurse. She handles a cardiac arrest on the ward calmly and well, goes home at nine, eats half a sandwich standing up, and at half past ten finds herself crying at an advert for car insurance, which has never before moved her to anything, while her body carries on running the emergency it thinks she is still in.

    So after something stressful, give your body a clear sign that it’s over. A walk round the block works, or a hot shower, or one song played loud in the car on the way home; the body takes its cue from what you do far more than from what you tell it.

    Dig deeper: the stress response

  2. Stress depends on what you have to meet it.

    The same deadline lands on two colleagues on a Thursday afternoon. One has a quiet evening and a takeaway menu. The other has a seven-year-old at home with a temperature and a partner away in Leeds until Saturday. On paper it’s one task. Guess which one is awake at 3am.

    Stress grows when a demand looks bigger than what you’ve got to meet it with, whether that’s time, energy, money, help, skill or sleep. That’s why a small thing tips you over on a bad day. It’s also why giving someone more support can shrink their stress without changing the job at all.

    You could say “It’s less the task than how little I’ve got left today.” “What would make this feel more doable?”

    When something feels huge, I’d write two lists side by side, one for what it asks of you and one for what you’ve got, and then ignore the first list for a minute and ask what would make the second one a line longer.

    Dig deeper: demands and resources

  3. The ladder: three everyday states.

    The ladder is a picture of the states your body moves between in a day. Near the bottom you’re calm and connected, breathing easily and able to hear something hard without bristling. Higher up you’re revved up, tense, and small things start to feel urgent or personal. Then there’s running on empty, which feels flat and slow, with the words just out of reach.

    Most people go up and down it many times a day. A grandfather minding his toddler granddaughter is calm at two o’clock, revved up by four (she has found the felt-tips) and running on empty by six. Neither of them has changed. Only the hour has, and how much afternoon is left in him.

    The Nervous System Ladder (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks) is a thirty-second check that gives you a best guess at where you are. If you’d rather not use a screen, set three reminders on your phone for today and, each time one goes off, notice which rung you’re on and do nothing else about it.

    You could say “I’m revved up right now.” “I’m running on empty. Can this wait till the morning?”

    Dig deeper: the ladder

  4. When you’re flooded, thinking goes offline.

    At the top of the stress curve your body is in full alarm, and the things a hard conversation needs most (careful thinking, listening, seeing the other side) get much harder to reach. Lots of people call this being flooded. You might say something you don’t mean, freeze, or want nothing except to be out of the room.

    Two adult siblings start sorting their late father’s things one wet Saturday. Within twenty minutes they’re shouting about a standard lamp that neither of them even likes. The real subject, that he’s gone, sits in the boxes around them and nobody says it.

    A flooded person is still a decent person whose body has to come down before the talk can go anywhere. It helps to know your own flood signs in advance. Heat in the face is common. So is a racing heart, or the room narrowing, or a voice in your head that has gone very loud and very certain. Notice two at once and you have your cue to stop.

    You could say “I’m too flooded to listen well. Can we stop for twenty minutes and come back at four?”

    Dig deeper: flooding

  5. Stress adds up, like a tank filling.

    Picture a tank that holds everything you’re already carrying today. The traffic goes in. So does the meeting that overran, the noisy shop, the text from your mum that just says “Call me when you can.” It’s all one tank, and by the evening something tiny makes it overflow and gets the blame for the whole lot.

    A fifteen-year-old explodes when he’s asked to empty the dishwasher. Later, from a friend’s mum at the school gate, his own mum finds out that his closest friendship fell apart at lunchtime, over something said in a group chat, and the dishwasher had simply been the next thing anyone asked of him.

    Small daily hassles count as much as big events here, which surprises people. (I can fill mine in one loud restaurant. That’s how I’m wired, and the About page on the website says more.) Before you react to a small thing in the evening, ask how full you were before it happened. Part Two, Chapter III has a quick way to tell.

    You could say “My tank was full before I got home. That wasn’t really about you.” “Rough day? You don’t have to explain.”

    Dig deeper: why stress adds up

    Professor Puddles

    Stress fills up a little at a time, like a puddle in a long spell of rain. Five quick questions tell you how full yours is today.

    Workpaper WP-02: How much are you carrying? spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-02

  6. Settle the body first.

    You can’t think your way out of a body in alarm, but you can help the body come down, and the thinking usually follows. Slow breathing with long out-breaths works for a lot of people. So does moving, humming something you know by heart, steady pressure like a heavy blanket, or just leaving the noisy room. What works is personal, which is why it’s worth finding your own short list on a calm day rather than in the middle of a row. A manager feels her heart going before she has to give some difficult feedback, so she walks once round the car park, breathing out slowly, and goes in a little steadier than she would have been.

    Put your list on your phone. The Calm-Down Kit (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11) helps you build it, and if you only keep one line from this section, keep “body first, words second”.

    Dig deeper: settling the body

  7. Rest isn’t one thing.

    An hour on the sofa scrolling can leave you more tired than when you sat down. That’s because recovery comes in different kinds. There’s sleep, and there’s switching off from work in your head, and real relaxation, and doing something absorbing that you enjoy, and the plain feeling of being in charge of your own time, and none of them stands in for the others.

    Two housemates have friends round on a Saturday night for a curry and the quiz on the telly. One wakes up on Sunday refreshed. The other spends the whole of Sunday alone with a library book and the door shut, and comes out at teatime feeling like herself again. Company restores some people and drains others, and neither of them is doing rest wrong.

    Ask yourself which kind of tired you are: body-tired, people-tired, brain-tired or feelings-tired. Then pick a rest that matches, rather than the one you always default to.

    You could say “I need quiet rest tonight rather than people rest. It isn’t about you.” “What kind of tired are you?”

    Dig deeper: kinds of rest

    Sugarfoot

    Rest can be a nap, a walk or ten minutes of quiet music. Find the kind that suits you, and keep it somewhere you can reach it.

    Tool: Cool-down corner: calm sounds and music spreadloveandacceptance.com/soundscapes

  8. zqaxunderstandingx2xstressxxsleepqz

    Sleep and stress feed each other.

    Stress makes sleep harder, and poor sleep makes stress land harder. After a short or broken night, small things feel bigger, tempers are shorter and people pull away from each other. This one is well studied. In a brain-scan study by Yoo and colleagues (2007), one night without sleep made the brain’s alarm centre react more strongly to upsetting pictures.

    In a daily study by Gordon and Chen (2014), couples reported more conflict after nights of poor sleep. In experiments by Ben Simon and Walker (2018), people who had missed a night’s sleep kept others at a greater distance and felt lonelier.

    Saoirse comes off her third night shift at the care home and bursts into tears over a parking ticket. Her sister says, “You’ve barely slept. Let’s sort it out on Thursday.” By Thursday it’s a parking ticket again, annoying and payable, and she pays it online during her lunch break.

    You can’t always fix sleep, but you can notice when it’s part of the story. Before a hard conversation, ask whether you’ve both slept, and if you haven’t, pick another time. At night, try the same few calm steps before bed in the same order, so your body learns the signal. If poor sleep goes on for weeks, talk to a doctor, because sleep problems are common and often treatable.

    You could say “I slept badly, so if I’m short with you today, that’s why.” “Can we talk about this after we’ve both slept?”

    Dig deeper: sleep and stress

  9. Stress is easier to carry when it’s shared.

    People calm each other down. A steady voice, a hand on the shoulder, or just a quiet person in the same room can help a nervous system settle. Saying your state out loud helps too, because “I’m stressed about work” stops your partner wondering whether it’s about them.

    A father tells his ten-year-old over fish fingers, “I’m a bit stressed about money this month. Sorting it is my grown-up job, and you’re not in trouble.” Over the next few days the boy stops tiptoeing round him and starts bringing his maths homework to the table again.

    Tonight, tell one person your state in one sentence, then ask how they are and listen to the answer.

    You could say “I’m stressed, and it isn’t about you.” “Would a hug help, or some space?”

    Dig deeper: stress between people

Monday, 7:58am

Six minutes after the snap, your partner is by the door, still patting their pockets. “Sorry,” you say. “My tank was full before you opened your mouth. Your keys are on the bathroom shelf, by the way.” They laugh and ask if it’s been a rough start. The bus is still late. The shoe is still missing. But the two of you are on the same side of the morning again.

In everyday life

Living on your own means nobody’s there to notice when you’re running on empty, so build rest into the week before you need it. With a partner, agree a pause word on a calm day, plus the rule that whoever pauses names a time to come back (One of you wants to talk now, the other needs space, spreadloveandacceptance.com/pursue-withdraw, has more on this). A child can’t settle until the nearest grown-up does. Your calm is something they borrow for years before they can make their own. And at work, a flooded colleague can’t take in feedback, so waiting an hour usually beats pushing on.

Some people run on empty for reasons built into their lives, like shift work, a long-term illness or caring for someone. What that calls for is a different setup. More effort won’t do it (see Different hours, spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours, and Caregivers, spreadloveandacceptance.com/caregivers). If you have ADHD, keeping track of everything can quietly fill the tank before breakfast. Get the remembering out of your head and into the world, with labelled alarms and one hook for the keys, and plan hard talks for your better time of day. More in the full chapter (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-2-stress-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

People often think all stress is bad. It isn’t. Short bursts help you rise to a challenge, and the harm comes from stress that never gets a recovery. Others think that being calm means not being upset, when you can be calm and sad, or calm and very firm. Pausing gets mistaken for avoiding, but a pause with a time to come back is how you finish a talk well, and avoiding is the pause that never comes back. Rest gets called lazy, though bodies and minds that never recover tend to break down. And short replies with a flat face are read as not caring, when far more often they mean someone is worn out.

If you want to help someone else with this

Nobody in the history of the world has calmed down because they were told to. A lower voice, slower words and a steady presence do far more. So does taking one job off someone’s list, which beats any pep talk. Ask what kind of help they’d like (practical help, company, a distraction or some space) instead of guessing. Don’t debate with someone who’s flooded; offer a break and a time to come back, because the facts will still be there in twenty minutes. And if someone has been running on empty for weeks, say so kindly and help them find support.

You could say “You seem really stretched. Is there one thing I could take off your plate?” “We don’t have to sort this now. Shall we pick it up after dinner?”

When to get more help

Stress is normal. Constant stress that never lets up is a warning sign. It may be time to see a doctor, counsellor or other trained professional if:

  • you’ve felt exhausted, dread-filled or numb most days for several weeks, even after rest;
  • you can’t sleep, or sleep but never feel rested;
  • you have physical signs that worry you, such as chest pain, constant headaches or stomach trouble (always get chest pain checked straight away);
  • you’re relying on alcohol, drugs or other habits to get through the day;
  • you feel you can’t cope, or have thoughts of harming yourself. If that is happening now, contact your local emergency number or a crisis line.

If the stress comes from being afraid of someone, such as how they will react, what they will do or whether you are allowed to leave, that is not ordinary stress. Your body may be warning you. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) has free, private help.

This chapter is general education, not medical advice or diagnosis.

Part Three · Chapter 3

How we see each other: perception, bias, and the stories we tell

Why two people can watch the same moment and come away with two different stories, and how to see others, and yourself, a little more fairly.

In this chapter

  1. Seeing is a best guess
  2. You see what you’re looking for
  3. We fill the gaps with stories
  4. We judge ourselves by our reasons, and others by their actions
  5. Quick shortcuts can lead us astray
  6. Everyone feels like the one who sees clearly
  7. “Us” and “them” changes what we see
  8. Ask, don’t guess
  9. In everyday life
  10. Common mix-ups
  11. If you want to help someone else with this
  12. When to get more help
  13. Tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

In short

  • Seeing is a best guess. Your brain fills in a lot of what you think you see and hear.
  • We fill gaps with stories, and the story often feels like a fact.
  • We judge ourselves by our reasons and others by their actions, and that gap causes a lot of hurt.
  • Asking is kinder and more accurate than trying to read someone’s mind.

Wednesday, 12:15pm

You wave at a colleague across the canteen, tray in one hand. She looks straight through you and walks off. All afternoon you wonder what you did, running back through Monday’s meeting, until at four o’clock she messages to say sorry for not stopping; she’d just had a call about her dad. She never saw you wave.

How feelings work (page 16) and Stress and the nervous system (page 30) look inward. This chapter looks outward, at how we see other people, why misunderstandings are so common even between kind and clever people, and what helps. Before I built any of this I spent my career as a government auditor, walking into situations where nobody could tell me straight what had happened. Almost everyone, it turned out, was doing their best with the piece of the picture they could actually see. That’s more or less this chapter.

Some of the tools elsewhere depend on it. Who did what (the Preface to Part Two, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/preface) exists because everyone sees their own effort more clearly than other people’s, so two honest guesses of “I do about 60%” can add up to well over 100%, and one shared page settles it. Rewind the talk (Part Two, Chapter III, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-3) slows down the habit of judging ourselves by our reasons and others by their actions. And the Chat analyzer follows this chapter’s last idea, that asking beats guessing.

  1. Seeing is a best guess.

    Your eyes and ears take in far less than you think, and your brain fills in the rest from what it expects. Most of the time this works well, and fast. It also means that what you see is partly what you expected to see, so two people can watch the same moment and honestly see different things.

    Two parents watch their son in an under-12s match on a freezing Sunday morning. One sees him giving up. The other sees him being careful with the ankle he went over on last week. Same boy, same touchline, same flask of tea. Next time you’re sure what someone meant by a look, think of two other things it could have meant.

    Things to tell yourself “This is what I see, and there may be more to it.” “What else could this be?”

    Dig deeper: perception as a best guess

  2. You see what you’re looking for.

    Attention is like a torch in a dark room. You see what it lights up and can miss what it doesn’t, even when it is right in front of you. If you are looking for proof that someone doesn’t care, you will notice every missed call and none of the little kindnesses.

    A woman decides in her first week that her new manager doesn’t like her. For a month she notices every short email he sends (there are a lot; he writes short emails to everyone). She somehow misses the fact that he gave her the best project on the team. If there’s someone you’re struggling with, write down one kind thing they do each day for a week. It’s an odd exercise, and it tends to change what the torch finds.

    Things to tell yourself “What might I be missing?” “If I were looking for the opposite, what would I see?”

    Dig deeper: the torch of attention

  3. We fill the gaps with stories.

    When we don’t know why someone did something, the mind makes up a reason fast. A late reply becomes anger and a closed door becomes rejection, and the story arrives feeling like a fact. Memory works this way too, because each time we remember something we rebuild it a little, so two people can honestly remember the same evening differently.

    A friend doesn’t reply for two days, and by the Sunday evening you’ve decided she’s fed up with you and drafted, then deleted, a message saying so. She was camping in Snowdonia with no signal, and comes back with photos of a sheep.

    You could say “The story I’m telling myself is that you’re upset with me. Is that right?”

    When something someone did hurts, write down the story you’re telling yourself, then one other story that would also fit.

    Dig deeper: stories and memory

  4. We judge ourselves by our reasons, and others by their actions.

    When you are late, you know why, whether it was the traffic, a phone call or a child who lost a shoe. When someone else is late, you only see the lateness, and it is easy to decide they are careless. We all tend to blame other people’s character for things that are really about their situation.

    A driver cuts in front of you on the ring road and you call him an idiot, not quite under your breath. The next week, rushing to the hospital because your mum has had a fall, you cut someone up yourself, and you know exactly why, and you’d like them to know it too.

    Thoughts you could try “What might be going on for them that I can’t see?” “If I did this, what would my reason be?”

    Dig deeper: actions and reasons

    Professor Puddles

    We know our own reasons and only see other people’s actions. Writing out their side, in their words, is a fair way to even that up.

    Tool: Rewind the talk spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder

  5. Quick shortcuts can lead us astray.

    The brain uses shortcuts to save time, and many are useful. Some lead to unfair judgements, such as a first impression that colours everything after it, a bad moment that outweighs ten good ones, or a quick guess about someone from their age, accent, looks or group. Everyone has these shortcuts, and the trouble starts when nobody notices them.

    A housemate decides on day one that the new tenant is messy, because of one box left in the hall. Every bit of mess after that counts as proof. Her own mug collection on the landing goes unseen. Pick one person you’ve made your mind up about and look for one thing that doesn’t fit.

    Things to tell yourself “Am I looking for proof of what I already think?” “Would I judge this the same if someone I like did it?”

    Dig deeper: shortcuts and bias

  6. Everyone feels like the one who sees clearly.

    Most of us feel that we see things as they really are and that anyone who disagrees must be missing something, or not thinking straight. The other person feels exactly the same about you, and each of you can see the other’s lens more easily than your own.

    Two adult siblings argue about how their parents raised them, and each insists they are just being realistic, which is true of what each of them lived through.

    Words you could use “I think we’re both seeing this from where we stand. Can you tell me how it looks from yours?”

    In your next disagreement, explain the other person’s view back to them until they agree you’ve got it, and only then give yours. You’ll find it slows everything down, which is rather the point.

    Dig deeper: why we each feel like the realist

  7. “Us” and “them” changes what we see.

    People split into groups quickly, even over tiny things. We tend to see our own group as varied and full of individuals and other groups as all the same, and we give our own side the benefit of the doubt. Spending real time with people from the other group, as equals, is one of the best ways to soften this.

    At one depot the night shift calls the day shift lazy and the day shift calls the night shift sloppy, and has done for as long as anyone can remember. After a joint training day with a bad buffet and a fire drill, people start using each other’s names. It doesn’t fix everything. It does stop the notes on the kettle.

    Things to tell yourself “Would I say this about one of ‘us’?” “Who in that group do I actually know?”

    One small step. Have one real conversation this month with someone from a group you tend to see as “other”, and ask about their day before you ask about their views.

    Dig deeper: us and them

  8. Ask, don’t guess.

    Imagining yourself in someone’s shoes is a kind start, though research suggests it doesn’t make us much more accurate about what they think, while asking does. A simple, curious question like “What was that like for you?” works better than the cleverest guess.

    A grandmother thinks her teenage grandson hates visiting, because he’s always on his phone at her kitchen table. One Sunday she asks. He’s been messaging a friend who is having a hard time, and he likes being at her house because it’s calm, and because of her apple crumble, though he wouldn’t have said so if she hadn’t asked.

    Ways to say it “Can I check what you meant?” “What was going on for you?” “I might have this wrong. How did it look from your side?”

    Dig deeper: seeing more fairly

Thursday, 12:20pm

You see your colleague in the canteen again, and this time you go over and ask how her dad is. She tells you about the hospital, and the waiting, and the car park charges, and you end up sharing a table until the end of the break.

In everyday life

We tell stories about ourselves too, and “I always mess things up” is usually built from a few bright memories that leave a great deal out. After years together, partners tend to stop checking and start assuming. And “I know what you meant” can do a lot of quiet damage in a long relationship. Children are often labelled early as the difficult one or the easy one, and the label becomes a lens that only sees what fits. With ADHD, attention is pulled by whatever is new or urgent and can lock on hard, so someone may truly not have seen or heard. It helps to get their attention first and to put requests in writing. More in the full chapter (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-3-seeing-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

Nobody just sees things as they are. Everyone sees through a lens, and knowing that is where fairness starts. Memory isn’t a recording either; it’s rebuilt each time, so two honest people can remember the same evening differently and both be telling the truth. Giving someone the benefit of the doubt doesn’t mean ignoring what happened. It means checking the story before you decide, and if something hurtful keeps happening, that matters. And a face or a tone is a clue to what someone meant. Faces and tones vary a lot between people and between cultures, so a face is a weaker clue than it feels.

If you want to help someone else with this

Start with how they feel. Make sense of the feeling first, and only then ask whether there might be another way to see it. Offer information rather than verdicts: “I know she had a hard week” helps more than “You’re being unfair to her.” Check your own guesses out loud (“I assumed he was annoyed. I’ll ask”), which shows how it’s done. Be careful with labels for children and colleagues, because they stick and then shape what everyone sees. And believe people about their own experience. Seeing other angles never means telling someone that what happened to them didn’t happen.

Words to try “That sounds really hurtful. Do you know what was going on for them?” “It might be worth asking. Want to plan what to say?”

When to get more help

Seeing other people’s side is a strength. It should never mean doubting yourself when you know something is wrong. If someone often tells you that what you saw, heard or remember didn’t happen, that you’re “too sensitive” or “imagining it,” and you find yourself unsure of your own mind, take that seriously. It can be part of controlling behaviour. Signs to look out for (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) and Not safe at home? can help, privately.

It may also help to talk to a counsellor or other trained professional if you notice you often feel others are against you, find it hard to trust anyone, or keep getting stuck in the same painful stories about yourself. Those patterns are common and understandable, and they often change with support.

This chapter is general education, not diagnosis or therapy.

Part Three · Chapter 4

How communication works: meaning, listening, repair and messages

Talking feels simple because we do it all day, yet every message has to travel from one mind to another, and a lot can change on the way. This chapter follows that journey and looks at what helps a message arrive the way you meant it.

In this chapter

  1. Meaning is made between two people
  2. Every message says two things
  3. Listening is something you do
  4. Check, don’t guess
  5. Hard things land better when they start soft
  6. Mix-ups are normal. Repair is the skill
  7. Messages lose their tone on the way
  8. Different styles aren’t wrong styles
  9. Small talk has a job, and it can be short
  10. In everyday life
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. When to get more help
  14. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  15. More for your situation

In short

  • Meaning is made between two people. What you say and what they hear can differ without either of you being wrong.
  • Every message says two things, the words themselves and what they seem to say about the two of you.
  • A short question saves a long misunderstanding, so check before you guess.
  • Mix-ups are normal, and repairing them is the skill. Small talk is allowed to be short.

Thursday, 8:15am

Ana texts her brother: “Can you call me when you’re free?” She means there’s no rush and she has a small question about the weekend. He reads it on the top deck of the 8.10 and spends the whole ride, eleven stops, wondering who is ill.

Small habits help a message arrive: listening, checking, starting softly, repairing quickly. A few ready-made lines make small talk easier for anyone who dreads it. And three tools elsewhere lean on this chapter. Say it so it lands (Part Two, Chapter IV, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-4) asks for what happened, how you feel and one clear request, because every message carries a second message about the relationship. The 90-second daily check-in (Part Two, Chapter I, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-1) keeps repairs small and frequent. And the Chat analyzer’s whole-conversation view shows where a written conversation lost its tone.

  1. Meaning is made between two people.

    Words don’t carry meaning on their own. The speaker has a meaning in mind, and the listener builds their own from the words, the tone, the timing and everything they already expect. Most of the time the two match well enough. Sometimes they don’t, and neither person can see the gap from where they’re standing.

    A manager writes “Let’s chat tomorrow” to a new starter, meaning a friendly catch-up and possibly a biscuit. He spends the evening convinced he’s in trouble and rereads his last three emails looking for the mistake.

    You could say “I think what I meant and what you heard might be two different things. Can we check?”

    Dig deeper: how meaning travels

  2. Every message says two things.

    There is what you say, and there is what it says about the two of you. “You’re late” is a fact about time, and it can also mean “I was worried” or “I don’t matter to you.” People often argue about the fact when the hurt is in the second layer.

    I take one eight-word sentence apart on the website’s About page: “don’t worry about it, I’ll sort it out.” Said kindly, in passing, it’s reassurance. Said for the third time that month about the same job, it also says a job has no owner and a decision has been put off again. Both layers are in the sentence. Or take a housemate asking whether she used his pan. It’s a question about a pan, and underneath it’s a question about whether his things are respected here, which no amount of talk about the pan will settle. Next time a small thing stings, ask what it seemed to say about us.

    Words you could use “I don’t really mind about the pan. I think I wanted to know my stuff matters here.”

    Dig deeper: the two layers of a message

  3. Listening is something you do.

    Hearing happens by itself. Listening is a choice, and most of us do it partly in order to reply, so we can fix or defend or advise or tell our own story. Real listening means following what the other person is trying to say and letting them know you got it before you add anything of your own.

    A thirteen-year-old says school is pointless. Her dad starts explaining, at some length, why it isn’t, and she stops talking and goes upstairs. The next time she says it, he bites his tongue and asks, “Pointless how? Tell me about today,” and she talks for twenty minutes, mostly about a supply teacher and a seating plan.

    Ways to say it “So what I’m hearing is... Have I got that right?” “Do you want ideas, or do you want me to just listen?”

    In one conversation today, wait until the other person has finished, then say back what you heard before you reply. It’s harder than it sounds.

    Dig deeper: what good listening is

  4. Check, don’t guess.

    Once we know something, it’s hard to imagine not knowing it. So we leave out steps, assume the other person can tell what we mean, and guess what they meant instead of asking. We do it most with the people we know best. A short check costs a sentence. A wrong guess can cost a whole evening.

    Two friends agree on “something low-key” for a birthday. One pictures a Chinese takeaway on the sofa in pyjamas. The other books a quiet table at the Italian place and irons a shirt. Both are disappointed, and both thought it was obvious.

    Words to try “Just so I’ve got it right, you mean...?” “When you say soon, do you mean today or this week?”

    Dig deeper: why we guess, and how to check

    Professor Puddles

    Checking takes ten seconds and saves an evening. When you’re ready to reply, this workpaper helps you say it so it lands.

    Workpaper WP-09: Say it so it lands spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-09

  5. Hard things land better when they start soft.

    How a hard talk begins often shapes how it ends. A complaint about one thing (“The bins weren’t taken out”) is easier to hear than a criticism of the person (“You never help”). A simple shape works for most hard things, which is to say what happened, how you feel and what you would like.

    A woman wants her eighty-one-year-old father to stop driving at night. She has “You’re not safe any more” on the tip of her tongue. She leaves it there and says, “You had two near-misses last month and I lie awake worrying. Could I drive us in the evenings?”

    You could say “What happened was... I felt... Could we...?”

    Dig deeper: saying hard things kindly

  6. Mix-ups are normal. Repair is the skill.

    Even close, kind people misunderstand each other all the time. What keeps a relationship steady is noticing and fixing it, with something like “That came out wrong” or “Can we start again?” Small repairs, made often, build trust far faster than big apologies made rarely.

    In the supermarket a stranger snaps “Excuse me!” when your trolley blocks the tins, and you snap back. A second later you add, “Sorry, long day,” and she smiles and says hers has been too, and you end up talking about the price of coffee.

    Words you could use “Can I try that again?” “I think I took that the wrong way. What did you mean?”

    Dig deeper: how repair works

    Sugarfoot

    A mix-up isn’t the end of anything. Come back, sit close, and go through it a step at a time.

    Tool: Rewind the talk spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder

  7. Messages lose their tone on the way.

    A text or email carries the words without your face or your voice, so the reader fills in the tone with however they feel right now, and a tired reader hears a tired, cross message. Short replies, missing greetings and late-night timing all get read as meaning something.

    In the group chat for the school summer fair, one parent replies “Fine.” to the plan for the tombola. Two others decide she’s annoyed. She was typing one-handed while stirring a pan of soup.

    Ways to say it “Quick reply. I’m not cross!” “This isn’t urgent. Any time this week is fine.”

    Before you send your next tricky message, read it out loud in the grumpiest voice you can manage. If it sounds harsh, add a warm word. (This is my favourite test in the whole book, and it takes four seconds.)

    Dig deeper: texts, email and tone

  8. Different styles aren’t wrong styles.

    Some people say exactly what they mean. Others hint, and expect you to read between the lines. Some talk fast and overlap; others need a pause to think. Families and cultures and different kinds of minds all shape this, and a clash between two styles is usually a matter of translation rather than of anyone being difficult.

    Asked whether the report is ready, an autistic employee says, “No, I need two more days.” Her manager hears bluntness until they talk about it, after which he starts to find her clarity a relief.

    Words to try “I’m quite direct, so if I sound blunt, it doesn’t mean I’m cross.” “It helps me if you say exactly what you need.”

    Dig deeper: styles, cultures and minds

  9. Small talk has a job, and it can be short.

    Small talk (“Cold today, isn’t it?” “Busy weekend?”) isn’t really about the weather. Its job is to say that you see the other person and that the two of you are okay. In 1923 the anthropologist Bronisław Malinowski called this “phatic communion”, talk whose main purpose is bonding more than information. Small moments like this matter more than people expect. Sandstrom and Dunn (2014) found that people who had a short, friendly exchange with a coffee-shop barista felt more belonging and a better mood than people who kept it purely efficient.

    Small talk is hard work for many people, though, including many autistic people, shy or anxious people and people speaking a second language. The rules are unwritten, and it uses energy that some people would rather keep. A few ready-made lines, sometimes called social scripts, take the guesswork out, and keeping it short is allowed.

    A dad who dreads the school gate keeps three lines ready: “Morning! How’s your week going?”, then “Oh, nice,” and finally “Right, I’d better get going. See you Friday.” Some mornings he still sits in the car with the radio on until the bell goes. Most days he gets through it, and one of the other dads now saves him a space by the railings.

    You could say “Morning! How’s your week been?” “How do you know Nico?” “Oh, how was that?” “Lovely to see you. I’d better get on.” And to opt out kindly, “I’m not great at chit-chat, but it’s really nice to see you.”

    Try this. Write your own three lines, one to open, one follow-up question and one to close, and use them once this week. If you would rather skip ahead to a real topic, “Can I ask you about something I’m actually curious about?” works too.

    Dig deeper: small talk and social scripts

Thursday, 9:02am

Ana’s brother rings the moment he’s off the bus. “Who’s ill?” She laughs and says nobody, she only wanted to know whether he’s free on Saturday to help move a wardrobe. He laughs too, a little shakily. The following week her text reads, “No rush and nothing’s wrong. Quick question about Saturday, call when you’re free.”

In everyday life

On your own: how you talk to yourself

You also send yourself messages all day, from “Typical, I always mess this up” to “That was hard, and I handled it.” The same ideas apply, so notice the tone, check whether the message is fair and repair it when it is harsh. Catch one harsh sentence you say to yourself today and rewrite it the way you would speak to someone you like.

zqaxunderstandingx4xcommunicationxxwithxothersqzWith other people

Between partners, “We never go out any more” sounds like a complaint about evenings, and underneath it may mean “I miss you,” so answering that layer goes further than defending the calendar. “Stop that!” tells a child what not to do without saying what to do instead, while “Feet on the floor, please” is easier to follow. In meetings, silence is often taken as agreement until a quieter colleague says later that she never agreed, and a round of “Anyone see it differently?” catches this early. “Are you eating properly?” is care in one generation’s language and checking up in another’s.

  • Feedback at work. Talk about the work rather than the person, with one recent example of what good looks like. Then ask, “What’s been getting in the way?” When you’re the one receiving it, “Thanks. Can I think about it and come back tomorrow?” is a fine first answer. The full chapter (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-4-communication-in-depth) walks through a whole performance conversation.

Common mix-ups

“If they loved me, they’d just know” is the big one. Closeness makes us check less without making us understand any more, so saying it clearly is a kindness, and no test of love. Listening isn’t agreeing, either. You can understand someone completely and still see it differently, and the understanding comes first. A repair doesn’t mean you’re admitting to being the bad one; it just says it didn’t go the way you wanted, and either person can make one. And texts feel safer for hard things because they’re easier to send. They’re also much easier to misread, so for anything tender, add warmth, or talk.

If you want to help someone else with this

Maybe a friend keeps having the same argument with their partner, or your teenager feels nobody listens. You can’t communicate for them, but you can help.

  • Listen first. The most useful thing is often to be the person who really hears them, without fixing.
  • Help them separate the two layers, by asking what it was about and what it seemed to say about the two of them.
  • Offer the simple shape of what happened, how they feel and what they would like, and let them find their own words.
  • Stay out of judging the other person’s character. You only hear one side, and they may make up next week.
  • Notice if it’s more than a mix-up. If they seem afraid of the other person, gently share Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety)

Words you could use “Do you want me to just listen, or help you think about what to say?”

When to get more help

Most mix-ups can be eased with the ideas here. Some situations need more.

  • When talking makes things worse every time, a couples or family counsellor can slow conversations down and help both people be heard.
  • When you’re afraid of how someone will react, that isn’t a communication problem. Clearer words are not the fix, and you don’t have to keep trying. Not safe at home? lists free, private help, and signs to look out for (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety#signs) may help you name what’s happening.
  • When someone is always “misunderstanding” you in ways that make you doubt your memory or your sense of what happened, talk with someone you trust outside the relationship.
  • When speaking or understanding is hard for you every day, because of anxiety, a hearing or language difference, or how your mind works, a doctor, speech and language therapist or counsellor may help. Needing support is not a failing.
  • If you’re overwhelmed right now, start with Upset right now (spreadloveandacceptance.com/upset-right-now).

Workpapers, tools and reading on the website

Try one of these this week with one real conversation. Say it so it lands (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-09-say-it-so-it-lands) helps you shape a hard sentence, Rewind the talk (spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder) walks you back through a talk that went wrong, and the wiring card (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wiring-card) puts how you communicate on one page.
