Part Three · Chapter 5

Attachment, trust and belonging

Why we need each other, how the bonds we had early on shape what we expect today, and how trust and belonging are built and lost and built again, one small moment at a time.

In this chapter

  1. Belonging is a basic need
  2. Early bonds teach us what to expect
  3. Patterns, not boxes
  4. Trust is built in small moments
  5. Feeling safe with someone calms the body
  6. Fitting in isn’t the same as belonging
  7. When trust breaks, rebuilding takes time
  8. You can start building connection from wherever you are
  9. If you’re a teenager
  10. In everyday life
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. When to get more help
  14. Reading on this site
  15. More for your situation

In short

  • Belonging is a basic need. Feeling lonely or left out is a signal, like hunger.
  • Early bonds set expectations that can change. What we learned about being cared for can soften over time.
  • Trust grows in small moments. Doing what you said, again and again, matters more than big gestures.
  • You can start small, with one friendly exchange or one kept promise.

Sunday, 9:30pm

Kai sent a long message to a friend at lunchtime, four paragraphs about his new job and a question at the end. It says “Read 12:47”. No reply. By teatime he has gone from thinking she’s busy to thinking she’s annoyed, and by half nine he’s wondering whether anybody really likes him at all. The friend, meanwhile, is at her nephew’s sixth birthday party at a soft-play centre, with her phone in her coat pocket under a pile of other coats.

Two tools elsewhere rest on this chapter. One owner per job (Part Two, Chapter II, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-2) works because trust is built from small promises kept, and a named owner turns “someone will probably do it” into a promise people can rely on. The monthly look-back (Part Two, Chapter V, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-5) looks at the month and keeps both people out of the dock, because feeling safe is what lets anyone say what went wrong.

  1. Belonging is a basic need.

    People need to feel connected, the way we need food and sleep. When we feel left out, it can hurt in a way that feels almost physical (Naomi Eisenberger and colleagues, 2003). That hurt works like hunger, telling us to reach for connection.

    Rhea moves to Manchester for work. She’s busy and doing well, and by the third month she feels flat and teary every Sunday afternoon, when the office is shut and nobody in the city knows her well enough to ring. This week, reach out to one person, even if it’s only a short “thinking of you”.

    Things to tell yourself “Feeling lonely says I need connection, like anyone does.”

    Dig deeper: why we need each other

  2. Early bonds teach us what to expect.

    As children, we learn from the people who cared for us whether others will come when we need them. If help usually came, we tend to expect it. If it came sometimes, or rarely, we may learn to cling harder or to stop asking. These lessons are a starting point that later relationships can change. This is the idea of attachment, first described by John Bowlby (1969) and studied by Mary Ainsworth and colleagues (1978).

    Watch a toddler at the park. He runs off towards the ducks, runs back to check his grandmother is still on the bench, runs off again a bit further, comes back, goes further still. He’s braver each time because he knows exactly where she is.

    You could say (to a child) “I’m right here. Go and look, and come back whenever you want.”

    Think of one person who was a safe base for you, at any age, and what they actually did.

    Dig deeper: what attachment is

  3. Patterns, not boxes.

    As adults, some of us worry a lot about being left, and reach out more when we feel unsure. Some of us pull back when things get close, and need more space. Many of us feel mostly secure, and most of us mix all three.

    These are patterns that can soften and change, especially in steady, kind relationships. Cindy Hazan and Phillip Shaver (1987) first described them in adults, and later work, such as R. Chris Fraley and colleagues (2015), suggests they work as sliding scales.

    When things feel tense, Ronan wants to talk it through straight away. His wife Clara needs to go quiet first, usually in the garden. He reads her quiet as a sign she’s leaving; she reads his questions through the back door as pressure. Once they see the pattern, they agree that Clara will say “I need an hour, and I’m coming back,” and Ronan will wait, which he finds very hard for about the first month.

    Words you could use “I’m not going anywhere. I just need some quiet. Let’s talk at eight.”

    Dig deeper: anxious, avoidant and secure

  4. Trust is built in small moments.

    Trust rarely comes from big gestures. It grows from small, ordinary things done again and again, like doing what you said, and being the same person on a hard day as on a good one. Honestly, it’s a bit boring. That’s why it works.

    A new team member says she will send the figures by Thursday, and she does. The next week she warns early that something will be late. By the third month her manager trusts her completely, and he would struggle to name a single moment when it happened.

    Ways to say it “I said I’d do it by Friday. I’m running late, so here’s where it’s at.”

    Dig deeper: how trust grows

    Professor Puddles

    Trust grows in small moments that repeat. This workpaper helps you notice the little rituals you already have, and keep them going.

    Workpaper WP-15: Keep your little rituals alive spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-15

  5. Feeling safe with someone calms the body.

    Being with someone we trust can settle our nervous system. In one study, holding a trusted partner’s hand calmed the brain’s response to threat (James Coan and colleagues, 2006). A calm voice, a hand to hold, or just someone nearby can make a hard moment easier to bear. It works both ways, so we can be that safe presence for others too, often without saying much.

    After a panic attack, Kieran’s friend doesn’t try to fix anything. He sits next to him on the step outside the flats and says, “Take your time. I’m here,” and they stay there until Kieran’s breathing slows.

    Words to try “You don’t have to talk. I’ll just sit with you.” “Would company help right now, or quiet?”

    Notice who helps you feel calmer, and tell them. “I always feel better after seeing you” is a lovely thing to hear and almost nobody says it.

    Dig deeper: a safe haven

  6. Fitting in isn’t the same as belonging.

    Fitting in means changing yourself to be accepted. Belonging means being accepted as you are. Teams, families, clubs and communities can offer either. Being left out of a group hurts even when the group doesn’t matter much to us, and real belonging grows where people feel safe to be themselves and to speak up.

    At a new job, Ola laughs at jokes she doesn’t find funny and orders a lime and soda “for the drive” so nobody asks why she doesn’t drink, and she goes home exhausted every Friday. At her book club, in the back room of the library on alternate Tuesdays, she says what she really thinks of the book, and people ask her to say more.

    You could say (in a group) “I see it a bit differently. Is it okay if I say why?” “Has everyone had a chance to say something?”

    Dig deeper: groups, work and community

  7. When trust breaks, rebuilding takes time.

    When someone lets us down badly, trust doesn’t come back with one apology. It returns slowly, as words are matched by actions over time. The person who broke trust can own what happened and be patient. The person who was hurt can decide, at their own pace, whether and how much to trust again.

    Two adult sisters fall out after one tells a private story at a family dinner, for a laugh. The apology is a start, and what slowly rebuilds trust is the months afterwards, when the story never comes up again and the sister checks before sharing anything.

    Words you could use “I know sorry isn’t enough. I’ll show you, and you can take whatever time you need.”

    Dig deeper: rebuilding trust

  8. You can start building connection from wherever you are.

    If you feel alone right now, big friendships can feel a long way off. Belonging can start much smaller than that: a chat with a neighbour, a regular class, an online group about something you love. Even small, light contact with people we barely know can lift our mood (Gillian Sandstrom and Elizabeth Dunn, 2014).

    After his divorce, Martin starts saying more than “thanks” to the man at the coffee stall outside the station. A few weeks later they’re talking football every morning, mostly about Stoke’s defence. It’s a small friendship. It makes Mondays easier.

    Ways to say it “I’m new around here. Is there anything you’d recommend?” “I loved what you said in the group. Would you like to get a coffee sometime?”

    Dig deeper: building connection

    Tidbit

    One small hello is a fine start. If you can’t think of one, there’s a tool that picks one for you.

    Tool: Stay close: one small idea spreadloveandacceptance.com/bonding

Monday, 8:10am

Kai’s phone buzzes with an apology. Her phone was in her coat all day at her nephew’s party, she loved the message, and is he free for coffee on Thursday? Kai thinks about how far last night’s story ran, and decides that next time a reply is slow he will send a light “No rush, just thinking of you” and leave it there.

If you’re a teenager

Ezra is sixteen when he sees a photo of his three closest friends at the cinema and finds out there is a group chat he isn’t in. It hurts like a punch, because being left out really does register a bit like pain. He drafts something sharp and deletes it, then messages one friend instead, saying he’s a bit gutted not to be asked and asking whether he did something. It turns out they thought he would be at football. One of the friendships really is drifting, though, and that is allowed to hurt too.

Words to try “Bit gutted not to be asked. Did something happen?” “I’d like to come next time, even if I can’t always make it.” “I miss how we used to be. Are we okay?”

Dig deeper: more worked examples

In everyday life

When one partner texts a lot while apart and the other forgets, agreeing on one goodnight message can keep both feeling connected. A child who acts up at pick-up may simply be letting go of a long day with the safest person they know. A friend who always cancels may be overwhelmed, and “Is it easier if we do something short?” keeps the door open. At work, a team where mistakes can be admitted without blame builds trust faster than one where everyone hides them, and in a shared house, one simple weekly meal can turn people who share a kitchen into people who look out for each other.

zqaxunderstandingx5xbelongingxxonxyourxownqzOn your own: belonging with yourself

Belonging also includes how you treat yourself. If you are kind to yourself on a bad day, you carry a small safe base wherever you go, and people who learn to comfort themselves often find it easier to let others in, because they are less afraid of being let down. You are allowed to need people, and a lonely day is hard without being a forecast. On my own (spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own) has more for people living alone.

Common mix-ups

  • “Needing people means I’m needy.” Everyone needs connection, including the people who hide it well.
  • “My attachment style is fixed for life.” Patterns can change, especially through steady, kind relationships and reflection.
  • “Jealousy and checking up show how much they love me.” Reaching for reassurance is human, and so is asking for something out of care for the relationship. Controlling who someone sees, or checking their phone without agreement, is not love and is not an attachment style. See signs to look out for (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety).
  • “If I forgive, I have to trust again straight away.” Forgiving and trusting are different. Trust can return slowly, or not at all, and that’s your call.

If you want to help someone else with this

Be steady. Turn up when you said you would, which matters more than any big gesture. If someone says they feel alone, listen before you remind them how many friends they have. Invite, and keep inviting; people who feel left out may say no a few times, and a warm invitation with no pressure still counts each time. In groups, notice who is on the edge and ask their view. And leave the labels out. Telling someone they’re “so avoidant” or “so clingy” has never helped anyone, as far as I can tell, while “what would help?” often does.

You could say “I’m here, and I’m not going anywhere.” “We’re having a few people over on Friday. No pressure, but I’d love you to come.”

When to get more help

  • If loneliness has lasted a long time, or comes with low mood, hopelessness or thoughts of not wanting to be here, please talk to a doctor or a mental health service. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number or see Upset right now (spreadloveandacceptance.com/upset-right-now).
  • If fear of being left, or of getting close, keeps hurting your relationships, a counsellor or therapist can help you understand where it comes from and how to change it.
  • If someone uses your need for them against you, by cutting you off from friends, checking where you are, or threatening to leave to get their way, that is not about attachment. Not safe at home? lists free, private help.
  • If trust was broken in a way that frightened you, you don’t owe anyone a second chance. Your safety comes first.

Reading on the website

Pick one small way to turn towards someone this week. Turning towards (spreadloveandacceptance.com/turning-toward), When one talks and one goes quiet (spreadloveandacceptance.com/pursue-withdraw) and How to apologise so it counts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/apology-languages) have more ideas.

6

Part Three · Chapter 6

Habits and change: why change is hard and how small steps work

Why it’s so hard to change, even when we really want to, and what actually helps: small steps, a kinder setup, patience with slips, and remembering that other people’s change belongs to them.

In this chapter

  1. Change is hard for good reasons
  2. Habits run on cues
  3. Start smaller than feels useful
  4. Change the setup, not just your willpower
  5. Being in two minds is normal
  6. Slips are part of change
  7. Change sticks when it fits who you want to be
  8. You can support change, but not force it
  9. In everyday life
  10. Common mix-ups
  11. If you want to help someone else with this
  12. When to get more help
  13. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

In short

  • Change is hard for good reasons. Habits save effort, so the old way is always the easy way.
  • A small step and a kind setup outlast willpower. Make the first step tiny and change what is around you.
  • Slips are part of change. A missed day tells you something about the plan and nothing about your character.
  • Other people’s change is theirs. You can support it, though you can’t force it.

Monday, 7:05am

The plan was a walk before work. The trainers are by the door. Somehow the phone is in your hand instead, and at 7:40 you’re still scrolling, past a video of a man restoring a rusty axe, next to a cup of coffee that went cold twenty minutes ago. By evening a quiet voice is telling you that you never stick to anything. What you actually ran into this morning was a habit with years of practice behind it, and it won.

This chapter is the reason several tools in these books are so small. One small step a week (Part One, Next, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/self-3-next) starts smaller than feels useful and decides ahead of time. The setup score and One owner per job (Part Two, Chapter II, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-2) change the setup rather than asking anyone for more willpower. And What keeps coming back? (Part Two, Chapter V, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-5) treats a repeat as information about the plan, because slips are a normal part of changing anything.

  1. Change is hard for good reasons.

    Much of what we do each day runs on autopilot. That saves energy, and it’s the whole reason habits exist. The downside is that the old way is always quicker and easier than the new one, so change asks your brain to do something effortful again and again, for weeks, until the new way becomes the easy one.

    Jodie wants to stop snapping at her children in the morning rush, and she means it every night. Every morning the same rush brings the same snap, somewhere between the lost reading book and the cold toast, because the morning has worn a groove deeper than her good intentions.

    Things to tell yourself “This is hard because it’s a habit.” “Old grooves take time to fill in.”

    Pick one thing you’d like to change and write down when it usually happens, where, and what’s going on just before. That’s the start of the next idea.

    Dig deeper: why change is hard

  2. Habits run on cues.

    Most habits have a trigger: a time, a place, a feeling, a person, or the thing you’ve just done. The cue starts the routine, and some kind of reward (relief, comfort, a little buzz) keeps it going. Once you know the cue, you can plan for it.

    A man notices that he reaches for the biscuit tin the moment he opens his laptop after dinner, hungry or not. The laptop is the cue. So he starts making a pot of tea before he opens it, and the biscuits, mostly, stay in the tin. For three days, each time your habit happens, jot down the time, the place, the feeling and what you were doing just before.

    Things to tell yourself “What happened right before I did that?” “What was I getting from it?”

    Dig deeper: cues and routines

  3. Start smaller than feels useful.

    Big goals are inspiring but easy to drop. Tiny steps feel almost silly, and they work because they are easy enough to do on a bad day. It helps to tie the new step to something you already do, as in “After I put the kettle on, I’ll…”, and to grow it only once it has stuck.

    Two housemates want a tidier kitchen. They’ve been promising each other a big Sunday clean since March, and it has happened once. So they agree instead that after dinner each of them wipes one surface. It takes two minutes. By the second week the hob has stopped being a source of tension, and by the fourth somebody has descaled the kettle without being asked.

    You could say “Let’s start with something tiny, and see if it sticks.” “After I ..., I will ...”

    Dig deeper: why small steps work

  4. Change the setup, not just your willpower.

    Willpower runs low when you’re tired or hungry. Your surroundings stay the same all day. So make the new habit easier, by putting it in sight or getting things ready the night before, and make the old one a little harder, by moving it out of reach or adding a step. I’d back a small change to the setup over a big push of effort almost every time.

    A teenager wants to sleep better and has tried for weeks to stop scrolling in bed. Then he starts charging his phone in the kitchen overnight, next to the bread bin, and within a week he’s asleep before midnight most nights. He grumbles about it. He also keeps doing it.

    Words you could use (to yourself or a partner) “What could we change about the setup so this gets easier?”

    Dig deeper: shaping your setup

    Professor Puddles

    Changing the setup is often easier than changing a person. At home, that can be as simple as one owner for each job.

    Workpaper WP-03: One owner per job spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-03

  5. Being in two minds is normal.

    Part of you wants to change and part of you doesn’t, and the reluctant part usually has its reasons. The old habit may give comfort, or protect you from something. Pushing harder against that part rarely works, while listening to it often does.

    Asif wants to drink less, but he also loves Friday evenings in the pub with his team. When he asks himself what Friday gives him, the answer is friends, laughter and a way to unwind, so he keeps the Friday and switches to alcohol-free after the first pint. Nobody at the table notices, or if they do, nobody says.

    Thoughts you could try “What does the old habit give me?” “What would make the change worth it to me?”

    Try two lists, one of what you like about how things are and one of what you’d like about changing. Both lists are allowed, and the first one is usually more honest.

    Dig deeper: readiness and mixed feelings

  6. Slips are part of change.

    Nearly everyone who changes something slips back sometimes, and one slip doesn’t undo your progress. What often does the damage is the thought that follows, the “I’ve blown it, so why bother?” Treating yourself kindly after a slip makes it more likely that you will start again.

    After three calm weeks, a dad shouts at his son over homework. That night he sits on the end of the bed and says, “I shouted, and I’m sorry. I’m working on it.” The next evening they do the homework at the kitchen table with the radio on, and nobody raises their voice.

    Things to tell yourself “A slip is one moment out of many.” “What made today harder, and what can I plan for next time?”

    Decide now, while things are going well, what you’ll do after a slip: one kind sentence to yourself, and one small step to start again.

    Dig deeper: slips and starting again

    Tidbit

    A slip is a stumble, not a fall. Try the tiny step again tomorrow. A game for small kind acts can make the practising easier.

    Tool: Gentle games: the Re-check Drive (calm football) spreadloveandacceptance.com/recheck-drive

  7. Change sticks when it fits who you want to be.

    Change made only to please others, or out of shame, is hard to keep. Change that connects to what you care about, to the kind of person you want to be, has deeper roots, and each small action becomes a vote for that person.

    A woman who keeps meaning to be better at keeping in touch starts thinking of herself as someone who shows up for her friends. Sending one voice note on a Sunday evening becomes part of who she is, and some weeks it turns into an hour on the phone.

    Things to tell yourself “Who am I becoming with this step?” “This matters to me because...”

    Dig deeper: values and who you’re becoming

  8. You can support change, but not force it.

    It is natural to want the people we love to change, perhaps to drink less or look after themselves better. Their change belongs to them, though, and pressure tends to make people dig in. It helps more to say clearly what you need, ask what would help, and notice their small steps out loud.

    A colleague keeps missing deadlines. His teammate has the lecture about being organised all ready to go, and skips it. She asks what would make the handover easier, and the two of them set up a shared checklist that he now updates every Friday before lunch.

    Ways to say it “I can’t change this for you, but I’d love to help if you want me to.” “I noticed you did that this week. That really helped.”

    Dig deeper: change with other people

Two weeks later, 7:05am

The trainers are still by the door, but the phone charges in the kitchen overnight now, and the plan has shrunk to shoes on and out to the end of the road. Some mornings that is all you manage. Most mornings it turns into a walk past the allotments and back. On the Thursday you miss, the voice starts up again, and you tell it that tomorrow you will get as far as the end of the road.

In everyday life

Take one couple who want to spend less time on their phones in the evening. Earlier attempts failed because each of them watched the other, so this time they agree on a basket by the door where both phones go at nine, with one exception for whoever is on call for an elderly parent. The first week is awkward, and on the Wednesday one of them sneaks a look at the football scores. By the third week the basket has become part of the furniture, and the evenings have a shape again, with a film, a crossword or an early night.

Big life changes, a move or a new baby, break old routines, which is disruptive and also a good moment to start new habits. If you have ADHD, make the cue impossible to miss, do the step the moment it appears and make the reward come straight away. Expect the novelty to wear off, and swap the method when it does instead of blaming yourself. More in the full chapter (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-6-change-in-depth).

On your own: a kind plan for change

If you are working on something alone, the ideas fit into one small plan. Choose one change, the one that would make the most difference or the one that feels most doable. Give it one cue, written as “After I ___, I will ___.” Make one tweak to your setup so it is easier to start, decide on the smallest version you could still do on a tired day, and write down one kind sentence to use after a slip. The self path (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path) and Know yourself, next walk through this step by step.

Common mix-ups

“If I really wanted it, I’d just do it” is the cruellest of these, and it’s wrong. Wanting is only the start; habits, setup, tiredness and stress all have a vote. Then there’s the famous 21 days. There’s no magic number. In one study, led by Phillippa Lally (2010), it took about two months on average, with a very wide range. Being hard on yourself doesn’t keep you on track either. Harshness tends to make people give up, and kindness makes it easier to try again. And routines don’t have to mean being rigid. For a lot of people, autistic people especially, routines are what make life manageable, and change can respect that.

If you want to help someone else with this

Ask before you advise, perhaps with “Would ideas help, or would you rather just talk it through?”, and help them find their own reasons by asking what would be different for them if this changed. Practical help with the setup (a lift to the gym, say) often does more than encouragement alone. Notice small steps out loud and be kind about slips. Look after yourself as well, because you can care deeply and still set limits on what you will put up with.

Words to try “I’m on your side with this. What would help?” “You’ve done this three days running. That’s not nothing.”

When to get more help

  • If a habit is harming your health or life, such as drinking, drugs, gambling, eating or self-harm, please talk to a doctor or a specialist service. Needing help with this is common and nothing to be ashamed of.
  • If you can’t stop even though you’ve tried many times, professional support can make a real difference. It isn’t a sign of weakness.
  • If change feels impossible because you’re exhausted or low most days, that may be burnout or depression. A doctor or counsellor can help.
  • If someone is demanding you change in ways that frighten you, or punishing you when you don’t, that isn’t support. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private help.
  • If you’re overwhelmed right now, start with Upset right now (spreadloveandacceptance.com/upset-right-now).

Workpapers, tools and reading on the website

Pick one tiny change and try it for a week. The 90-second daily check-in (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-13-daily-check-in), the quick checks (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks) and the self path can help you keep track.

7

Part Three · Chapter 7

Self-worth, shame and self-compassion

Why your worth isn’t a score you keep earning, how shame differs from guilt, and why being kind to yourself makes it easier to grow.

In this chapter

  1. Your worth isn’t a score
  2. Guilt says “I did a bad thing.” Shame says “I am bad.”
  3. Shame makes you want to hide
  4. The inner critic is trying to protect you
  5. Self-compassion isn’t letting yourself off
  6. Comparing yourself pulls your worth outside you
  7. You can own a mistake without drowning in it
  8. Worth is learned between people, and we can give it
  9. In everyday life
  10. Common mix-ups
  11. If you want to help someone else with this
  12. When to get more help
  13. Tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

Thursday, 11:20pm

You sent the wrong file to the whole team, last quarter’s figures instead of this one’s. Priyanka spotted it within four minutes, sent the right one round and said “no worries!” with an exclamation mark. Hours later you’re still awake and replaying it, and the voice in your head has moved on from the file altogether. It’s telling you that you’re useless, and that everyone knows it now.

This chapter is about how self-worth and shame work, and then about what you can do with them, on your own, at home, with friends or at work. None of it is a diagnosis. Take what helps.

  1. Your worth isn’t a score.

    A lot of us carry a quiet scoreboard. We’re worth something when we’re useful, or liked, or slim, or busy, or top of the class, or never any bother. Psychologists call these “conditions of worth”, and the trouble with them is that any score can drop. If your worth goes up and down with each day’s results, every bad day feels like a verdict on you as a person.

    Pam taught Year 4 for forty years. In the September after she retires she feels lost in a way she can’t explain to anyone, wandering round the big Tesco at ten on a weekday morning. Nothing is wrong. For four decades being needed was how she knew she mattered, and the bell has stopped ringing. Try finishing the line “I feel okay about myself when I…” three times, and look at what you wrote; those are your scores. Noticing them is plenty for now.

    Dig deeper: worth that doesn’t have to be earned

  2. Guilt says “I did a bad thing.” Shame says “I am bad.”

    Guilt is about something you did, so it points somewhere useful: say sorry, put it right. Shame is about who you are, which feels impossible to fix, and so it makes people hide, freeze, blame someone else or lash out. Research on the two feelings, such as June Tangney and Ronda Dearing’s (2002), suggests guilt is the one more likely to lead to repair.

    A twelve-year-old knocks his mum’s favourite mug off the side, the one with the hare on it from Whitby. Guilt tells him to own up and offer some of his birthday money towards a new one. Shame tells him he ruins everything, and he wraps the pieces in yesterday’s newspaper and pushes them to the bottom of the kitchen bin. So next time you feel bad about something, ask which one it is. If it has turned into who you are, try to shrink it back to the one thing you did, and then ask what would make that thing right.

    Dig deeper: guilt, shame and repair

  3. Shame makes you want to hide.

    You feel shame in the body before you think it: a hot face, eyes down, a sinking stomach, the wish for the floor to open. It can also come out sideways as sudden anger or a closed, cold face, which is how a small comment starts a big fight. In a meeting someone asks, mildly enough, “Didn’t we already cover this?” and his colleague snaps back at him. That evening she realises the snap had nothing to do with the question; she had felt stupid in front of everyone.

    It helps to learn your own shame signs. Next time you suddenly want to disappear, or to bite, you can name it quietly to yourself, and sometimes say it out loud: “I think I felt embarrassed just then, and it came out sharp. Can I try again?”

    Dig deeper: how shame works in the body

  4. The inner critic is trying to protect you.

    That harsh inner voice usually started as protection. If you criticise yourself first, perhaps nobody else can get in a blow. If you’re hard enough on yourself, perhaps you’ll never fail again. It meant well. But a voice that only threatens keeps your body on alert, and it’s exhausting to live with.

    A young dad calls himself an idiot every time he forgets something for the baby, the wipes, the rabbit she won’t sleep without. It’s the word his own father used about him. The voice he hears in the car park at the nursery is an old one, borrowed years ago and never given back. Write down one thing your critic says often and ask whether you’d say it to a friend you love. Some people find it helps to answer the critic directly: “Thanks for trying to protect me. I can take it from here.”

    Dig deeper: the critic and the soothing system

  5. Self-compassion isn’t letting yourself off.

    Self-compassion means treating yourself the way you’d treat a good friend who’s struggling. One well-known model has three parts: kindness in place of attack, remembering that everyone struggles, and noticing the pain without drowning in it. Studies, such as one by Juliana Breines and Serena Chen (2012), suggest that people who are kind to themselves after a failure are often more likely to try to improve.

    Lindy fails her driving test for the third time, on the reverse round a corner again. In the test centre car park she tells herself that this is hard, that loads of people need more goes, and that she’ll practise that one manoeuvre on the industrial estate on Sunday mornings when it’s empty. Then she books another lesson. If it feels okay, put a hand on your chest or arm once today and say, slowly, “This is a hard moment. Other people feel this too. What do I need right now?”

    Dig deeper: what self-compassion is, and isn’t

    Sugarfoot

    Speak to yourself the way you’d speak to a friend having a hard day, slowly and kindly. Writing it down first helps.

    Tool: Write it through spreadloveandacceptance.com/write-it-through

  6. Comparing yourself pulls your worth outside you.

    Everyone measures themselves against other people; it’s how we work out where we stand. Feeds full of other people’s best moments make the measuring wildly unfair, though, and self-esteem that depends on being better than others swings about a great deal.

    Two old friends meet for a curry, one with a new house, the other renting a room in a shared flat. The renter spends the whole evening quietly ranking herself and misses what’s in front of her, which is that her friend is lonely in the new house and had wanted to talk about it. When you catch yourself comparing today, try swapping it for a question about the other person, like “How are you, really?” You’re comparing your inside with their outside, after all.

    Dig deeper: comparison and steady self-worth

  7. You can own a mistake without drowning in it.

    Owning a mistake gets much easier once it doesn’t mean you’re worthless. A simple shape helps. Say what you did, say what it did to the other person, say what you’ll do now, and stop. Beating yourself up afterwards proves nothing about how sorry you are; it just moves the attention back to you.

    A housemate forgot to pay her share of the broadband and it was cut off for the whole of a bank holiday weekend. She tells the others, “I forgot to pay, and that left you without internet all weekend. I’ve paid it and set a reminder for the 28th,” and that’s the end of it. Think of one small thing you still feel bad about and write your own three-part sentence. Then decide whether to send it or let it rest.

    Dig deeper: owning it, repairing it, letting it rest

    Professor Puddles

    Owning a mistake can be short and plain: what happened, that it was yours, what you’ll do. If it went wrong in a talk, Rewind the talk helps you find the words.

    Tool: Rewind the talk spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder

  8. Worth is learned between people, and we can give it.

    Children learn their worth from how they’re treated, and adults never quite stop learning it. The words matter. “You did a careless thing” leaves room to change, while “you’re so careless” shuts the door. Praise for effort and for who someone is, as well as for results, helps people feel they matter on bad days too.

    A team lead starts every project review by asking what the team learned rather than who got it wrong. Within six months, people are raising problems in week two instead of week ten, which saves everyone a great deal of Friday evening. Today you could say one thing to someone that has nothing to do with their results, even just “I’m glad I know you.”

    Dig deeper: how worth is given and learned

Your part, and only your part. You can’t control how other people judge you, or what you were taught about your worth growing up. You can control how you speak to yourself now, whether you repair what you can, and where you spend your time. Give your energy to people who treat you as someone who matters. More in Part One: who you are today (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/self-2-now)

Friday, 9:15am

You send one line to the team, sorry for the mix-up with yesterday’s file, right one attached. When the old voice starts up you answer it the way you’d answer a friend: you made a mistake and you fixed it, which is what a decent colleague does. Priyanka replies with a thumbs-up. Nobody mentions the file again, and by lunchtime you’ve mostly stopped thinking about it too.

In everyday life

Shame turns up in very ordinary places. Between partners, “You forgot to call” can land as “You’re a terrible partner”, and so the reply comes out as a defence instead of a sorry. A child who hears “You’re so naughty” learns something about who they are, while “That was a naughty thing to do” leaves them a way back. A friend who says yes to everything may be quietly burning out, because saying no feels like risking being dropped. At work, someone may sit on a small error for weeks because owning it feels like proof they don’t belong there.

On your own: a kinder voice to keep

You don’t need anyone else to start this. Notice how you talk to yourself and practise one gentler sentence. Catch the critic’s favourite words (“always”, “useless”, “pathetic”, “should”) and swap one of them for a plain fact, so “I’m hopeless” becomes “I was late twice this week.” On hard days keep a short list of what you did well, or simply did, and let getting up count. You’re allowed to be disappointed in what you did and still be on your own side.

Common mix-ups

People worry that self-compassion is self-pity. They feel different from the inside: self-pity says “only me, poor me”, while self-compassion says “this is hard, and other people go through it too”, which connects you to others rather than shutting you off. Others fear that being kind to themselves will make them lazy. The research leans the other way, because fear of your own attack is what makes people avoid trying and hide mistakes. And self-worth doesn’t mean thinking you’re great. It means you matter on the days you aren’t.

If you want to help someone else with this

Talk about what happened, never about what kind of person they are. Arguing with someone’s shame (“You’re not useless!”) can feel like being told they’re wrong to feel it, so try “It sounds like you feel really low about it. I don’t see you that way.” Helping them find one small thing they can do gives the feeling somewhere to go. And kindness on ordinary days, when nothing has gone wrong, teaches worth better than anything said in a crisis.

You could say “That sounds like it’s weighing on you. Want to work out one thing that would help?” “You don’t have to earn being cared about.”

When to get more help

Everyone feels shame and self-doubt sometimes. It’s worth talking to a doctor, counsellor or therapist if harsh thoughts about yourself are there most days, if they stop you working, eating, sleeping or seeing people, or if you feel you deserve to be hurt. Therapies such as compassion-focused therapy and cognitive behavioural therapy are built to help with exactly this.

If you are having thoughts of hurting yourself or not wanting to be here, please tell someone today. In the US and Canada, call or text 988. In the UK and Ireland, call Samaritans free on 116 123. In Australia, call Lifeline on 13 11 14. In New Zealand, call or text 1737. Anywhere else, findahelpline.com lists free helplines. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number.

If someone close to you keeps telling you you’re worthless, stupid or lucky to have them, that isn’t a self-esteem problem. It can be a way of controlling someone. Signs to look out for (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) and Not safe at home? have free, private help.

What to remember

  • Shame makes you want to hide.
  • Self-compassion isn’t letting yourself off.

Part Three · Chapter 8

Loss, grief and big life changes

What grief is, why it comes in waves, how it shows up in the body, and how to carry a loss, or a big change, without having to “get over it.”

In this chapter

  1. Grief is love with nowhere to go
  2. Grief comes in waves, not neat stages
  3. Grief lives in the body, too
  4. Some losses nobody sees
  5. People grieve in different ways
  6. You don’t have to let go
  7. Big changes are losses too, even the good ones
  8. Most people find a way through, and support helps
  9. Losing a partner in later life
  10. In everyday life
  11. If you want to help someone else with this
  12. When to get more help
  13. Tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

In short

  • Grief is love with nowhere to go. It hurts because the person, place or life mattered.
  • It comes in waves. A good week followed by a bad day is part of grieving, and it doesn’t send you back to the start.
  • You don’t have to let go. Many people keep a bond with the person they lost, and that is healthy.
  • Most people find a way through. Support helps, and some losses need more help than friends can give.

Saturday, 9:05am

Six months on, you’re doing fine, or so you tell people. Then in aisle seven you see the cereal your dad always bought, the one with the faded blue box that he said tasted of cardboard and ate every single morning anyway, and you have to leave your trolley where it is and go and sit in the car. Nobody around you knows why.

This chapter is for anyone who has lost someone or something, whether a person, a pet, a marriage, a friendship, their health, a home, a job, a country or a future they had pictured. It looks at how grief works and then at what can help. There’s no right way to grieve. Nothing here is a timetable, and if any of it doesn’t fit you, leave it.

  1. Grief is love with nowhere to go.

    Grief is what we feel when something we were attached to is gone, and it isn’t only for deaths. A divorce, a miscarriage, a diagnosis, a move, a friend who drifted away or children leaving home can all bring real grief. Its size usually matches the size of the bond, whatever other people think the loss ought to mean.

    When Bramble dies, his owner is shaken by how hard he takes it, and his friends at the pub tell him, kindly enough, that it was only a dog. That dog walked beside him along the same stretch of river every morning for twelve years, through two jobs and a divorce. The lead is still on its hook by the back door, and he can’t move it yet.

    It can help to say a loss out loud to yourself, especially one you’ve never called grief. “I’m grieving the friendship.” “I’m grieving the life we planned.” They’re small sentences, and they often bring some relief, because they give the feeling a name and a reason.

    Dig deeper: what grief is, and what counts

  2. Grief comes in waves, not neat stages.

    You may have heard of five stages of grief, running from denial through anger, bargaining and depression to acceptance. They came from listening to people who were dying, and they were never meant as steps that everyone follows in order. Most people swing back and forth, some hours deep in the loss and some hours getting on with life, and researchers who study grief see that swing as healthy. A widow laughs properly over a jacket potato with her sister on a Wednesday, feels guilty about it on the bus home, and cries all evening. The lunch was grief too.

    A small break from grief, a walk or a programme you like or a meal with a friend, takes nothing away from the person you lost. And when a wave comes, it does usually pass, even if it knocks you over first.

    Dig deeper: waves, and the swing between loss and life

  3. Grief lives in the body, too.

    Grief can bring tiredness, poor sleep, no appetite or extra appetite, aches, a tight chest, forgetfulness and a foggy head. Your brain is slowly learning that someone or something it expected to be there has gone, and that learning takes time and uses energy. A deputy head whose mother has died loses her car keys three times in one week and walks into a governors’ meeting on the wrong day, and she starts to worry that something is wrong with her memory. It’s grief fog. It eases as the months pass, though nobody can tell her exactly when.

    While it lasts, protect a few basics: one regular meal, a set bedtime, a short walk outside. It’s fine to tell people at work or at home, “I’m grieving, so I’m slower than usual. Could you send me a reminder?”

    Dig deeper: the grieving body and brain

  4. Some losses nobody sees.

    Some losses are hard to explain to anyone else. Someone may still be alive but changed by dementia or illness, or gone without having died, like an estranged parent or a missing relative. Other losses go unrecognised, such as the death of an ex-partner, a pregnancy loss or a friend you only ever knew online. A woman whose father has dementia still visits him at the care home every Sunday at two. He’s pleased to see her. He thinks she’s his sister. The dad who knew her is fading, and she is grieving someone who hasn’t died, which is a very lonely kind of grief because there’s no ceremony for it and hardly anyone notices.

    If a loss of yours had no ceremony, you can make a small one of your own by lighting a candle, writing a letter, planting something or visiting a place that mattered. You might also tell one person, “I’m grieving something people might not see as a loss. It is one for me.”

    Dig deeper: ambiguous and unrecognised grief

  5. People grieve in different ways.

    Some people grieve by talking and crying, and others by doing, whether that means fixing things, organising, working or building something. Neither way is more loving. Families often clash because one person thinks another isn’t grieving, when they’re grieving differently, and culture, faith, age and how your mind works all shape the way it comes out. After their son’s death, one parent wants to talk about him every evening. The other spends every weekend in the garage, restoring the old Raleigh he never got round to fixing. Each feels the other is getting it wrong. Each is grieving the same boy.

    A question can bridge the gap. “What has helped you most, even a little?” asked of someone who shares your loss, and listened to without correcting, often shows that the two of you want the same thing by different roads.

    Dig deeper: grieving styles and families

  6. You don’t have to let go.

    An older idea said that healthy grief meant moving on and cutting ties. Many grief researchers now see it differently. People often keep a bond with the person they lost, in memories, rituals, conversations in their head and values they carry forward, so the relationship changes shape without having to end. A teenager wears her grandfather’s watch to every exam, a heavy old thing that she has to push up her arm to write. She doesn’t believe in luck, and she’d find it hard to explain why the watch matters, except that it feels as if he’s in the room.

    You might choose one way of keeping a bond, such as cooking their recipe, telling a story about them at a family meal or keeping one of their habits. Some people find it helps to ask, in a hard moment, what the person they lost would have said.

    Dig deeper: continuing bonds

  7. Big changes are losses too, even the good ones.

    A new baby, a promotion, retirement, moving country, a child starting school, coming out or getting well after a long illness can all bring grief for the old life. Change often has three parts, an ending, a confusing time in between and a new beginning, and the middle part is both the hardest and the easiest to rush. A couple move to Bristol for a job they both wanted. Six months in, one of them feels low, then guilty for feeling low, because this was the plan and they’d toasted it with fizz. What they also lost was a circle of friends, a café where nobody had to ask what they wanted, and a whole way of life.

    You can be glad about a change and still miss what came before. For one change you are going through, it may help to write down what ended, what still feels unclear and one small thing that is new and good.

    Dig deeper: endings, the in-between, beginnings

    Professor Puddles

    When a change is hard to talk about, writing can come first. This is a quiet place to put the words down, at your own pace, and to send them only if you want to.

    Tool: Write it through spreadloveandacceptance.com/write-it-through

  8. Most people find a way through, and support helps.

    Research suggests that, over time, many people find they can live with a loss and still feel joy, even though they never forget. Being with people who let you talk, or let you stay quiet, helps. For some people, though, grief stays at full strength for a long time and makes daily life very hard.

    Doctors call this prolonged grief. It means a strong longing for the person, or being taken over by the loss, most days, still going many months after the death (6 to 12 months or more, depending on the guideline) and getting in the way of life. It has nothing to do with weakness, and there is specific help for it. A year after his wife died, a man still can’t go into their bedroom or face his friends, and his doctor refers him to a grief counsellor. Things begin to move, slowly, starting with one evening a week at his brother’s, where they watch the snooker and don’t talk much.

    On a good day, write down two people you could text on a hard one, and one place you could call if those people aren’t enough. If it has been a long time and nothing is easing, it is reasonable to say, “I think I need more help.”

    Dig deeper: resilience, support and stuck grief

Your part, and only your part. You can’t control the loss, how long grief lasts, or how other people react to it. You can control small things: eating something, resting, telling one person how you are, and saying no to what you can’t manage right now. That is enough for a hard season. More in Part One: who you are today (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/self-2-now)

Saturday, 9:40am

You sit in the car for ten minutes and let the wave come. Then you go back in. Your trolley is where you left it, next to the porridge, and you put the cereal in. At home you text your sister that you saw Dad’s cereal and cried in the car park. She replies straight away that the same thing happened to her with his aftershave in a chemist’s, and asks whether you can call tonight.

zqaxunderstandingx8xlossxxlaterxlifeqzLosing a partner in later life

After a long marriage the loss is in everything, from the empty chair to the jobs that were always theirs, the paperwork done alone and the first birthday and anniversary without them. Do one small thing at a time, and let one drawer count as a day’s work. It is fine to ask someone to sit with you while you fill in the forms.

Your grown-up children have lost a parent while you have lost a partner, and you may grieve on different timetables. If they start checking on you every day, that comes from love and worry. It isn’t control. You can still say what helps: “I love that you ring. Could we make it two evenings a week, and I’ll ring you if I need you?”

Dig deeper: the first year, and grown-up children

In everyday life

After a miscarriage, one partner may want to talk while the other goes quiet, and each can end up worrying that the other doesn’t care. A child may laugh and play the day after a funeral and then cry at bedtime, and both belong to grief. A friend who stops calling after your diagnosis is often stuck for words more than cold, and colleagues who avoid the subject when someone returns after a death can leave that person feeling as if the loss has been erased. A whole community can grieve together too, when a town loses its library or its factory.

On your own: carrying it gently

Grief can be lonely even with people around you. When you are carrying it alone, it helps to give the day a small shape, with one meal, one walk and one person you message. Expect harder days around birthdays and anniversaries, and plan something gentle for them. Writing to the person you lost, or about what you lost, can help too, and nobody else ever needs to read it. Some days the only goal is to get to tonight, and that is allowed.

If someone close to you has died. Grief and later life (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grief) goes further, with family after a loss, coming back to people, and a new chapter on your own. On a heavy night, the page called For a hard evening (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grief#hard-evening) may help.

If you want to help someone else with this

Show up, and then keep showing up. Support tends to flood in for two weeks and then stop, so a text at three months, or on a birthday, can mean a great deal. Offer something specific; “Can I drop off dinner on Thursday?” is far easier to say yes to than “Let me know if you need anything.” Say the name. Many grieving people find it a comfort to hear the name of the person they lost, and a memory of them, and if you’re unsure, ask. Leave out the explanations, because “Everything happens for a reason” and “At least…” tend to hurt, while “I’m so sorry. I’m here” rarely does. And if you’re upset too, lean on people further from the loss rather than on those closest to it. Comfort goes in towards the centre; venting goes out.

You could say “I don’t know what to say, but I’m here.” “I was thinking about your mum today. I remember her laugh.” “I’m going to the shop. What can I bring you?”

When to get more help

Grief is not an illness. But it’s worth talking to a doctor or a grief counsellor if, after many months, the pain isn’t easing at all, you can’t manage daily life, you feel life has no meaning without the person, or you are drinking or using other things to get through. Many hospices, faith communities and charities offer free bereavement support, including for children.

If you are having thoughts of not wanting to be here, please tell someone today. In the US and Canada, call or text 988. In the UK and Ireland, call Samaritans free on 116 123. In Australia, call Lifeline on 13 11 14. In New Zealand, call or text 1737. Anywhere else, findahelpline.com lists free helplines. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number.

If a loss involved violence, or you are grieving a relationship you left because you weren’t safe, Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) has free, private help, including after you separate (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety#after-separation).
