Part Three · Chapter 13

Anger: what it’s for and what to do with it

What anger is for, what to do in the hot minutes, how to repair afterwards, and how to tell when anger has turned into harm. For anyone, in any kind of relationship, or on your own.

In this chapter

  1. Anger is a signal about something that matters
  2. Anger often guards a softer feeling
  3. Anger rises in the body fast
  4. In the hot minutes: slow the body first
  5. Letting rip doesn’t empty it
  6. Step back and look from the outside
  7. Say it, don’t throw it
  8. After anger, repair
  9. When anger becomes harm
  10. If you’re a teenager
  11. In everyday life
  12. Common mix-ups
  13. If you want to help someone else with this
  14. When to get more help
  15. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  16. More for your situation

In short

  • Anger is a signal that something seems unfair, blocked or threatening. The feeling is allowed, and what you do with it is the part you choose.
  • The first minutes are about the body. Slow down, breathe out long, and step away with a time to come back.
  • Letting rip doesn’t empty anger. Shouting tends to feed it, while calming the body, putting it into words and repairing any sharp moments help more.
  • Anger that frightens, controls or hurts someone has become harm. That needs more help, and safety comes first.

Tuesday, 6:10pm

Your brother texts: “Can’t do Thursday after all, sorry!! Work thing.” Thursday is Mum’s hospital appointment, the one with the consultant, and this is the third time this month. Your jaw sets. Your face goes hot. Your thumbs are already typing “TYPICAL. You never…” and the message is one tap from sent.

Plenty of us were taught that anger was rude or dangerous, or grew up around anger that was frightening. Anger itself is a normal human feeling, though, and it very often points at something real. This chapter looks at how it works and then at what to do with it. It also sits under two tools elsewhere: the Calm-Down Kit (Part One, Now, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/self-2-now), which works because anger rises in the body first and slowing the body is what makes words possible, and letting a comment land before you react (Part Two, Chapter IV, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-4), which is the step back described further on.

  1. Anger is a signal about something that matters.

    Anger usually says that something is unfair, that someone is in your way, or that a line has been crossed. It pushes you towards a problem so you’ll change it. It can also land on the wrong person, or come out far bigger than the problem in front of it.

    Somebody keeps eating Shabnam’s lunch from the office fridge. Week one, she assumes a mistake. Week two, she writes her name on the box in marker pen. By week three her anger has told her clearly that a line has been crossed, and it’s the anger, frankly, that gets her to raise it at the Monday meeting. (It was the new starter. He thought the fridge was communal. He bought her a meal deal.) Next time you’re angry, finish this sentence privately: “I’m angry because something I care about, which is ___, seems ___.”

    Dig deeper: what anger is for

  2. Anger often guards a softer feeling.

    Anger can arrive first because it feels stronger and safer than what sits under it, whether that’s hurt or fear or shame or plain tiredness. Chapter 1 (page 16) calls this layers. The layer underneath usually tells you what you actually need.

    A father snaps at his sixteen-year-old for coming in an hour late. Under the anger is an hour spent at the front window, phone in hand, imagining the worst. When he tells her about that hour instead of the curfew, she hears it, and says sorry, and means it.

    You could say “I’m angry, and I think underneath I was really scared.” “I came across cross, but I think I’m actually hurt.”

    Dig deeper: what anger can cover

  3. Anger rises in the body fast.

    A hot face, a tight jaw, a pounding heart, a voice getting louder: that’s the body getting ready for a fight, and it can happen in seconds. When anger is high, careful thinking gets much harder, and so does listening. Chapter 2 (page 30) calls this being flooded, when you’re so stirred up that the thinking part of you goes quiet for a while.

    Halfway through an argument about whose turn it was to put the bins out, a woman notices her hands are shaking and realises she hasn’t heard a word her housemate has said for at least a minute. That’s her sign to stop. Learn your own early signs, two or three of them, like a tight jaw or talking faster, and treat them as your cue to slow down.

    Dig deeper: anger in the body

    Professor Puddles

    Anger moves faster than words. The Calm-Down Kit is a plan you make on a calm day, for the hot minutes.

    Workpaper WP-11: The Calm-Down Kit spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11

  4. In the hot minutes: slow the body first.

    When anger is high, settle your body before you try to sort anything out. Stop talking, or typing. Breathe out slowly, so the out-breath is longer than the in-breath. Unclench your hands, and if you can, move away for a while. A large review of 154 studies by Kjærvik and Bushman (2024) found that activities which calm the body, like slow breathing, relaxation and mindfulness, reduced anger, while ones that rev you up showed little or no benefit.

    A dad feels his temper going while he helps with fractions homework at the kitchen table. He says, “I’m getting frustrated, and that’s not your fault. I’m going to get a glass of water and come back in five minutes.” He comes back in five, and they finish the sheet together, and both of them get number six wrong.

    You could say “I’m too angry to talk well right now. I’ll come back at eight.” “I need ten minutes. I’m coming back to this conversation.”

    Make the plan on a calm day: your early sign, the words you’ll say, and where you’ll go for ten minutes. Upset right now? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/upset-right-now) has steps for the hottest moments.

    Dig deeper: what to do in the moment

  5. Letting rip doesn’t empty it.

    A lot of people believe anger works like steam, so that shouting or slamming a door or hitting a pillow lets it out and leaves you calmer. It’s a lovely tidy idea, and the research doesn’t support it. In a well-known study by Bushman (2002), angry people who hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who annoyed them ended up angrier than before.

    Going over what happened again and again in your head has a similar effect. In studies by Bushman and colleagues (2005), people who dwelt on a provocation were later more aggressive, even towards someone who only mildly annoyed them. Anger fades faster when the body is calmed and the mind has something else to do for a while.

    After a row with a colleague, a man spends his lunch break telling three different people how awful she is, and by the afternoon he’s angrier than he was at noon. The next time it happens he walks to the river and back instead, and by two o’clock he can think about the actual problem. If you catch yourself replaying an argument, set a timer for twenty minutes, do something absorbing, then come back to it.

    Dig deeper: venting and going over it

  6. Step back and look from the outside.

    Once your body has settled a bit, try looking at the moment as if you were watching from across the room. What happened? What might the other person have been dealing with? In experiments by Mischkowski, Kross and Bushman (2012), people who looked back on an annoying moment “like a fly on the wall”, instead of reliving it, felt less angry and acted less aggressively. Rethinking what happened, which psychologists call reappraisal (Gross, 1998), helps too.

    Furious that a friend has cancelled again, a woman imagines telling the whole story to a kind stranger on a train. Telling it that way, she remembers that her friend is caring for her dad, who has been in and out of hospital since June, and the anger turns slowly into worry. One way in is to write two lines about the moment with your own name instead of “I”: “Wes got angry because…” It feels odd. It also works.

    Dig deeper: stepping back

  7. Say it, don’t throw it.

    Anger is often a fair message sent in a hurtful way. Once you’re calmer you can still say you were angry, and why, without attacking anyone. A simple shape helps: what happened, how you felt, what you’re asking for.

    So instead of “You always let me down,” a woman says to her sister, “When you cancelled Mum’s appointment again, I felt really angry and alone with it. Can we make a plan for who takes her over the next three months?” It’s longer. It’s also the only version that ends with a plan. Write your angry message, then rewrite it in that shape before you send anything. Chapter 4 (page 59) has more on saying hard things.

    You could say “I was angry about what happened on Monday. Can I tell you why?” “When ___ happened, I felt ___, and what I’m asking for is ___.”

    Dig deeper: saying anger in words

    Sugarfoot

    Say it slowly, in one plain sentence. A soft start makes it far easier for the other person to hear you.

    Tool: Cool-down corner: soften a tense moment spreadloveandacceptance.com/tools/soften-a-tense-moment

  8. After anger, repair.

    Everyone gets angry, and most of us say something sharp now and then. What happens next matters a great deal. A short, real repair rebuilds trust, and it means naming what you did without a “but”, then saying what you’ll do differently.

    A grandmother shouts at her grandson when the blue vase from the hall table ends up in pieces, and he cries. An hour later she sits beside him on the stairs and says, “I shouted, and that was scary. You matter far more to me than the vase. I’m sorry.” He leans against her shoulder for a bit and then asks whether they can glue it. They try. It now has a visible crack and lives on the landing. Is there a recent moment when your anger landed on someone, and a short repair you could still make? Chapter 11 (page 157) has more on apologies that land.

    You could say “I was sharp with you earlier. That wasn’t fair, and I’m sorry.” “I’m still upset about what happened, and I also shouldn’t have spoken to you that way.”

    Dig deeper: repair after anger

  9. When anger becomes harm.

    Feeling angry is human. But some things done in anger are harm, whatever the feeling behind them: hitting, pushing, throwing things at or near someone, breaking their things, threatening, shouting so someone is scared, or using anger to control what another person does, wears, spends or who they see. People walking on eggshells around you is a sign too. Anger is never a reason someone deserves to be hurt.

    For example, a man realises his partner and children go quiet when he comes home in a bad mood. He doesn’t hit anyone, but they are afraid of him. He talks to his doctor and joins an anger course.

    You could say “I think my anger is scaring people I love. I want help with it.” (If it’s happening to you) “I’m frightened of how they get when they’re angry.”

    Try this. If this sounds like you, see Find a counsellor or therapist (spreadloveandacceptance.com/outside-help) and the Cool-down corner. If you’re afraid of someone else’s anger, Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private help.

    Dig deeper: when anger becomes harm

Your part, and only your part. You can learn your early signs, settle your body, say what made you angry in words, and repair when you get it wrong. You can’t make someone else calm down, and you don’t have to accept being shouted at, threatened or controlled. If someone else’s anger frightens you, getting safe matters more than working it out. Not safe at home?

Tuesday, 6:40pm

You put the phone face down on the arm of the sofa and walk round the block, breathing out long. Somewhere near the postbox on the corner you notice what’s under the anger. You’re tired, and you’re frightened about Mum. Back home you delete the capitals and write, “I’m really frustrated. This is the third time and I feel alone with Mum’s care. Can we talk tonight and make a plan?”

He reads it at 6:52. By ten o’clock there’s still no reply, and you go to bed not knowing who’ll drive her on Thursday. You sent the message you can stand behind. That part is done, even if the rest of it isn’t.

zqaxunderstandingx13xangerxxteensqzIf you’re a teenager

Maisie is sixteen, and at ten o’clock her dad takes her phone, right in the middle of a group chat about Saturday. She shouts and slams her bedroom door hard enough to rattle the picture on the landing. The next morning, calmer, she tells him it felt as if he didn’t trust her, says sorry for the door, and asks for ten minutes’ warning next time. He agrees, and adds that he’d much rather hear this over breakfast than through a door.

Being angry with a parent is normal, and arguments often feel most intense in the middle teens. A rule given out of care is not control, even when it feels unfair, and a calm request the next day works more often than a slammed door.

You could say “I’m too angry to talk properly. Can we talk tomorrow?” “I don’t mind the rule so much as how it happened.” “Could we try it for two weeks and then check?”

Dig deeper: more worked examples

In everyday life

Anger at yourself counts too. “I’m so stupid” is anger turned inward, and it helps to talk to yourself the way you would to a friend who’d made the same mistake (Chapter 7, page 100, goes further). With a partner, agree a pause word on a calm day, and a time you’ll always come back. Children copy what we do with anger far more than anything we say about it. At work anger is common and rarely spoken, and “I’m frustrated about the deadline change. Can we talk about what’s realistic?” keeps it useful.

If you have ADHD, anger can arrive fast and big and then go just as quickly, so plan for the speed: a three-word pause line like “Back in ten”, and a rule to wait before you send anything. If you’re managing a clash between two other people, hear each of them alone first and then together, always about what happened and never about each other. The fight is often about the setup, two people who both believe they own the same job. The full chapter has a worked example (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-13-anger-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

Anger itself isn’t a bad feeling. It’s normal and it carries information; it’s some of the things done in anger that cause harm. Letting it out isn’t the healthy option it sounds like, because shouting or hitting things tends to keep anger going. “They made me angry, so it’s their fault I shouted” mixes up two things: someone can do something unfair, and what you do next is still yours. And holding it in isn’t as safe as it looks. Anger swallowed for years tends to come out sideways, as coldness or sarcasm or a sudden explosion over a teaspoon, so saying it calmly and early is the safer route.

If you want to help someone else with this

Keep yourself safe first. If someone’s anger scares you, step away; you don’t have to stay and calm them down. Otherwise speak lower and slower, and leave the argument until they’ve come down. Then listen for the message under it. There’s often something fair in there, and you can take that part seriously while still saying that the way it was said wasn’t okay.

You could say “I want to hear this, and I can’t while we’re both shouting. Can we try again at seven?” “I can tell this really matters to you.”

When to get more help

Everyone gets angry. It may be time to talk to a doctor, a counsellor or an anger management course if:

  • your anger feels out of control, or you often regret what you do or say when angry;
  • people close to you seem nervous or walk on eggshells around you;
  • you have hit, pushed, thrown things, broken things or threatened anyone;
  • anger is hurting your work, your friendships or your health;
  • you are using alcohol or drugs to cope with angry feelings.

Help for anger works for many people: a review of anger treatments by Del Vecchio and O’Leary (2004) found medium to large benefits. It is good for your health too: a review by Chida and Steptoe (2009) linked anger and hostility with a higher risk of heart disease. Asking for help is a responsible thing to do. Find a counsellor or therapist (spreadloveandacceptance.com/outside-help#counsellor) lists places to start, some of them free, and the Cool-down corner helps in the hot minutes.

If you are afraid of someone else’s anger, that fear is an important signal. Not safe at home? lists free, private help. If you or anyone is in danger right now, call your local emergency number.

This chapter is general education, not therapy.

Part Three · Chapter 14

Personality, temperament and change across life

What personality is, where temperament comes in, how people change across their lives, and how to live and work with people who are made differently from you, without putting anyone in a box.

In this chapter

  1. Traits work like dials
  2. Temperament is the starting point
  3. Situations matter too
  4. Introvert and extravert is about energy, not liking people
  5. People change across life
  6. You can change on purpose, a little at a time
  7. Every trait has gifts and costs
  8. Differences are usually about fit
  9. In everyday life
  10. Common mix-ups
  11. If you want to help someone else with this
  12. When to get more help
  13. Tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

In short

  • Traits work like dials. Everyone sits somewhere along each one, and most people are near the middle.
  • Temperament is a starting point. Babies already differ in how active, cautious or easily upset they are, and what happens next matters too.
  • People keep changing. On average people grow steadier and more organised as they get older, and you can change on purpose, slowly.
  • Most clashes between personalities are about fit, and nobody has to be at fault.

Saturday, 3:00pm

It’s your aunt’s seventieth in the function room above the cricket club, and you’re standing quietly by the cake when she announces, loud enough for the whole room, that you were always the shy one. Everyone laughs. You smile along while something stings. You’re forty-two. You stand in front of thirty children every weekday morning at twenty to nine. So are you still the shy one? Were you ever?

We describe each other by personality all the time (laid-back, a worrier, the organised one) and descriptions like those have a way of hardening into boxes. This chapter is about how personality actually works, and what stays put and what moves. Two tools elsewhere build on it: the “How to talk to me” card and the style quiz (Part One, Now, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/self-2-now) describe how you lean on a few dials, which is more use than knowing which box someone put you in, and One owner per job (Part Two, Chapter II, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-2) arranges the jobs around people’s differences so nobody has to become someone else to share a home.

  1. Traits work like dials.

    Personality is the usual pattern in how you think and feel and act. Many psychologists describe it with five broad traits, often called the “Big Five”: openness (curious about new ideas and experiences), conscientiousness (organised and careful), extraversion (drawn to people and busy places), agreeableness (warm and cooperative) and emotional stability (how steady your moods are).

    The same five turned up in work such as McCrae and Costa (1987), whether people rated themselves or were rated by people who knew them well. Each one runs from low to high, and most people sit somewhere near the middle of most of them. That’s the bit the online quizzes tend to leave out. Two friends do one on a train and get told, with great confidence, that one is an introvert and the other an extravert; when they look at the actual scores, they’re four points apart and both near the middle. If you’re curious, mark where you think you sit on each dial from one to ten, then ask where a close friend would put you. The gap is often the interesting part.

    Dig deeper: the five dials

  2. Temperament is the starting point.

    Temperament is the part of personality you can see from very early on. Some babies are very active and some are calm. Some settle easily into new routines and some take their time. Some react strongly to noise or change. In their long-running study, Thomas and Chess (1977) described these early differences and the idea of “goodness of fit”, meaning how well a child’s temperament fits what the people and places around them expect of it.

    A toddler who is slow to warm up cries at every new playgroup. Her mum stops trying to coax her into the circle and lets her watch from her lap for ten minutes instead, a bit awkwardly, in a church hall that smells of squash. By the third week the little girl climbs down on her own and goes to the sand table.

    You could say “You like to watch first. That’s fine. Join in when you’re ready.” (to yourself) “I need time to warm up. That’s how I’m made.”

    Dig deeper: temperament and fit

  3. Situations matter too.

    Personality describes a pattern, and patterns have exceptions. The same person can be loud with family and quiet at work, or endlessly patient with toddlers and very short with call centres. A trait tells you what someone tends to do across lots of situations. It tells you much less about this one.

    A manager decides that a new colleague is cold. Then at the team’s charity football match she watches the same colleague in a borrowed bib, chatty, shouting encouragement at the goalkeeper, and on Monday she sits looking at the open-plan office wondering how much of what she’d seen was the room. Before you decide what someone is “like”, try to see them somewhere else, or at least ask them about somewhere else.

    Dig deeper: person and situation

  4. Introvert and extravert is about energy, not liking people.

    People who are more introverted often like people very much. What they find is that busy, noisy social time uses up energy, and they need quiet afterwards to get it back. People who are more extraverted tend to be topped up by company and busy places. Most of us are a mix, sometimes called an ambivert, and every point on the dial just needs different things to feel at its best.

    At about eleven at a wedding in a barn near Hexham, one partner wants to go on to the after-party in the village pub and the other wants bed and silence. So one goes for an hour and the other walks back to the hotel, and they meet at breakfast, one of them a bit hoarse, both of them happy.

    Words you could use “I loved tonight, and I’m out of social energy.” “Shall we go together, and I’ll head home at ten?”

    Dig deeper: introversion and extraversion

    Tidbit

    Some people recharge in a busy park and some under a quiet blanket. Both are fine. A short quiz can show you your own style.

    Tool: How you connect: the 2-minute style quiz spreadloveandacceptance.com/wavelength

  5. People change across life.

    Personality is fairly stable. It also moves. A large review by Roberts, Walton and Viechtbauer (2006) found that, on average, people become more organised, more emotionally steady and more confident with others as they move through adult life, with much of the change between 20 and 40. A later review by Bleidorn and colleagues (2022) found that emotional steadiness went on growing right across the lifespan. Big life events play a part, and so do the roles people take on and who they love.

    A man who was a nervous, disorganised student, the one who lost his keys every fortnight, is a calm, steady nurse in his forties, and his old school friends barely recognise him at the reunion. When they ask, he says that life kept asking him to cope and he slowly learned how. Write down one way you’ve changed in the last ten years, and what helped it happen.

    Thoughts you could try “Who I was at fifteen isn’t who I have to be now.” “People I knew years ago may have changed too.”

    Dig deeper: how personality changes with age

  6. You can change on purpose, a little at a time.

    If you want to change a trait, you can, slowly, mostly by acting differently in small ways again and again. In a study by Hudson and Fraley (2015), people who set goals to change one of their traits tended to move in the direction they wanted over sixteen weeks. A review by Roberts and colleagues (2017) found that therapy was often linked to lasting change too, especially towards more emotional steadiness.

    A woman who wants to be less shy at work makes one small plan: say one thing in each team meeting, even if it’s only agreeing with someone. For the first fortnight her heart pounds every time. After two months speaking up has become ordinary, and she has started to forget it was ever a plan. Pick one small action that fits who you’d like to be more of, like replying to messages the same day or saying hello first, and do it three times this week. Chapter 6 (page 87) has more on habits.

    Dig deeper: changing on purpose

  7. Every trait has gifts and costs.

    There’s no good personality. Each trait helps in some places and gets in the way in others. Very agreeable people are kind and easy to be with, and may find no almost impossible to say. Very conscientious people are the ones you’d trust with your keys, and they may struggle to rest. People high in openness love new things and can be bored rigid by routine.

    A very organised woman spends most of a year irritated by her relaxed housemate, his trainers in the hall and his “it’ll be fine”. Then the boiler packs in on the coldest night in January, and he’s the one who stays calm, finds an emergency plumber at ten o’clock and makes everyone hot water bottles from the kettle. Pick one trait of yours that people sometimes complain about, and write down a time it helped.

    Things to tell yourself “What is the gift in this trait, and what is the cost?” “What they do that annoys me might be the flip side of something I value.”

    Dig deeper: gifts and costs

    Professor Puddles

    Every trait has gifts and costs. Writing down what helps you on a one-page card turns a “flaw” into useful information.

    Tool: How you connect: how I like to be spoken to spreadloveandacceptance.com/wiring-card

  8. Differences are usually about fit.

    When two people with different personalities share a home or a family or a job, friction is normal. A tidy person and a relaxed one can both be right in their own way, and so can a planner and someone spontaneous, or a talker and someone who needs quiet. What helps is naming the difference and agreeing how to live with it, without either of you being the problem. Personality is also different from neurodivergence and from mental health conditions; if something feels bigger than personality, Chapter 9 (page 125) may help.

    A couple argue about every single holiday, because one wants every hour planned and the other wants to wander about and see what happens. This year they plan the mornings and leave the afternoons free. They still argue about the mornings. I’d count that as progress.

    Ways to say it “I think we’re just made differently here. What would work for both of us?” “I’m a planner and you’re not. Can we plan half and leave half?”

    Dig deeper: fit, not fault

Your part, and only your part. You can get to know your own mix, look after what you need, and practise one small change if you want to. You can’t change someone else’s personality, and you don’t have to change yours to be loved. If you’re always the one bending to fit, it’s fair to say so. Know your own wiring (spreadloveandacceptance.com/know-yourself)

Saturday, 5:30pm

As people start to drift off with foil-wrapped slices of cake, you think about sitting down next to your aunt and telling her about the thirty children. In the end you help clear the plates and say nothing. On the drive home you’re still turning it over, half annoyed with her and half with yourself. You wonder whether she’ll say it again at Christmas, and what you would like to say back if she does.

In everyday life

On your own

Knowing your own mix helps you build a life that suits you, with about the right amount of company and quiet. “I’m just not a people person” might be true, or it might be an old label worth testing at least once. With a partner, a shared plan (one of you does the bills, the other the holidays) usually works better than trying to change each other. A quiet friend who hardly texts may still care a great deal, so ask what kind of contact suits them. A child’s temperament says nothing about good or bad parenting, and adjusting to fit them is a skill you learn. And family roles like “the clever one” or “the difficult one” can stick long after they stop fitting. You’re allowed to grow out of them, even if your aunt hasn’t noticed.

Common mix-ups

You aren’t simply an introvert or an extravert. Most people are somewhere in the middle, and where you sit can shift with the setting and your mood. Personality isn’t set in stone by adulthood either; it keeps moving slowly across the whole of life. Online type quizzes are good for fun and conversation, and that includes the website’s own Wave Code, which shows four leanings on four dials, but they sort people into a handful of types when real people are spread along each dial. “They’re just difficult” often means “they’re different from me”, and it can hide stress or illness or a need nobody has asked about. And practising something new isn’t being fake. It feels unnatural at first, the way new shoes do, and becomes part of you over time.

If you want to help someone else with this

Drop the old labels. Notice if you still describe someone the way they were years ago, and look for who they are now. Ask instead of guessing: “What helps you recharge?” or “How do you like to plan things?” will tell you more than any theory about their personality. Notice growth out loud, because “You handled that so calmly” can show someone a change they hadn’t spotted in themselves. And describe the action rather than the person. “You’re so uptight” or “You’re just lazy” closes doors that a plain description of what happened would leave open.

Words to try “I used to think of you as the shy one. I don’t think that fits any more.” “What do you need to be at your best this week?”

When to get more help

Personality differences are normal and don’t need fixing. It may be worth talking to a doctor, counsellor or psychologist if:

  • a pattern in how you feel, think or relate to people keeps causing you or others real distress, across many parts of life;
  • you feel very unsure who you are, or your moods swing so much it’s hard to cope;
  • worry, low mood or fear of people is stopping you from living the life you want.

Please don’t diagnose yourself or anyone else with a “personality disorder” from what you read online. Those are clinical terms that only a qualified professional can use, after a proper assessment.

A personality trait never excuses controlling, frightening or hurtful behaviour. If you’re afraid of someone close to you, Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private help.

This chapter is general education, not a diagnosis or therapy.

Part Three · Chapter 15

Closeness and love: being known, at every age

How closeness grows, what it means to feel truly known, how love changes over the years, and how it looks in every kind of relationship, at every age, including for people on their own.

In this chapter

  1. Love comes in many forms
  2. Closeness grows from being known
  3. Closeness is built a step at a time
  4. Feeling understood matters most
  5. Old maps show up in love
  6. Love changes over time
  7. Love at every age
  8. Love is something you do
  9. If you’re a teenager
  10. In everyday life
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. When to get more help
  14. Reading on this site
  15. More for your situation

Friday, 10:30pm

You and Charlie have shared a home for eleven years. Tonight you’re both on the sofa and both on your phones, a cooking programme on in the background that neither of you is watching, and you realise you can’t remember the last time the two of you talked about anything except bills, the boiler and whose turn it is to cook. You love Charlie. You feel oddly alone in the same room.

This chapter is about closeness in all its forms, far beyond romance. It looks at what helps people feel near to each other, and why closeness fades and how it grows back, and it builds on Chapter 5 (page 74), on attachment and trust.

  1. Love comes in many forms.

    The ancient Greeks had several words for love, for friends, for family, for romantic partners and for strangers. People love in many ways today too. There are lifelong friendships, partners of any gender, people with more than one partner, chosen family, people who are asexual or aromantic and build deep closeness without romance or sex, and people on their own who pour love into friends, family, pets, work and community. A life can be full of love without a partner in it.

    A woman in her fifties who has never wanted a partner describes her best friend of thirty years as her great love story. They have been through two house moves, one cancer scare, a disastrous caravan holiday in Tenby and more Sunday phone calls than either of them could count. Try writing down three or more people you love, of any kind, and next to each one the way you show it. The list is usually longer than people expect.

    Dig deeper: the many forms of love

  2. Closeness grows from being known.

    Intimacy is about much more than touch or romance, and at its heart is being known. The psychologists Reis and Shaver described it as a back-and-forth, in which one person shares something real about themselves and the other responds in a way that leaves them feeling understood and cared for. In a diary study by Laurenceau, Barrett and Pietromonaco (1998), feeling that the other person really responded was a big part of what made everyday conversations feel intimate.

    Two brothers who mostly talk about football are driving to their dad’s care home when one admits that he finds the visits really hard. The other says he does too, and that he always feels guilty on the way home. It’s the longest conversation they’ve had in years, and it lasts all the way to the car park, where they sit with the engine off for another ten minutes. Sharing one small, true thing with someone you care about (a worry, a hope, something that made you happy this week) and noticing how they respond is the same thing on a smaller scale.

    Dig deeper: intimacy as being known

  3. Closeness is built a step at a time.

    People usually get close by sharing a little more, and then a little more, when it feels safe. In a well-known study by Aron and colleagues (1997), pairs of strangers who took turns asking gradually more personal questions, now known as the “36 questions”, felt closer after forty-five minutes than pairs who made small talk. The same idea works in friendships and long relationships, where closeness grows when both people take small, matched steps. Two new neighbours start with the weather and the parking, which in their street is a serious subject. A few months later one asks how the other’s mum is getting on. Some time after that, over the fence, one of them says, “Can I tell you what’s really been going on?”

    Next time you talk to someone you would like to know better, ask one question a little deeper than usual, such as what has been on their mind lately, and if they answer, share something of your own back.

    Dig deeper: building closeness step by step

    Professor Puddles

    Closeness grows when you know what feels like care to the other person, not just to you. A “What feels like care” card is a gentle way to find out.

    Tool: How you connect: what feels like care spreadloveandacceptance.com/love-languages

  4. Feeling understood matters most.

    What makes someone feel loved is often less about grand gestures and more about feeling understood. Researchers call this responsiveness, meaning noticing, understanding and caring about what matters to the other person, and it shows in small moments such as how you react to good news. Gable and colleagues (2004) found that people whose partners usually met their good news with real interest and warmth felt closer and more satisfied together. When a teenager announces that she’s been picked for the school band, her grandad puts the paper down, smiles, and asks which instrument and when the first concert is. She talks for twenty minutes, mostly about the trombone section. The next time someone shares good news with you, put your phone face down and ask two follow-up questions. That’s the whole method.

    Dig deeper: responsiveness

  5. Old maps show up in love.

    The patterns from Chapter 5 (page 74) often come out most strongly with the people we love most. Hazan and Shaver (1987) suggested that adult love uses the same attachment system as childhood bonds. When closeness feels shaky, some people reach harder for reassurance and others pull back to feel safe, and both are ways of protecting something precious. When his partner goes quiet, Leo texts five times in an hour, while his partner, who goes quiet in order to calm down, feels crowded. They agree that his partner will say, “I need an hour, and I’ll message you at eight,” and Leo finds, somewhat to his surprise, that he can wait for a known time. What he couldn’t bear was the not knowing. It’s worth noticing what you do when closeness feels shaky, and telling someone you trust what helps you feel safe again.

    Dig deeper: attachment in adult love

  6. Love changes over time.

    Early love is often intense, with racing thoughts and a lot of longing, and over the years it usually settles into something calmer and deeper. A review by Acevedo and Aron (2009) found that some people in long relationships still report strong romantic love, without the anxious, obsessive edge of early love, and that this was linked to being happier together.

    In experiments by Aron and colleagues (2000), couples who tried a new, mildly challenging activity together felt better about their relationship afterwards than couples given a dull task. After twenty-five years, one couple sign up for a pottery class at the community centre. They’re both terrible at it. They laugh all evening and bring home a bowl that won’t stand up, and on the way home one of them says it felt like a date. I’d take new over big: a new walk, a new recipe, a new café in the next town.

    Dig deeper: how love changes

    Sugarfoot

    Little rituals, like a Sunday walk or a goodnight text, keep love warm through the years. Look after the ones you already have.

    Workpaper WP-15: Keep your little rituals alive spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-15

  7. Love at every age.

    Love looks different across a life. Teenagers’ first loves can be huge and real, and adults juggle love with work and children and, often, ageing parents. Many older people choose to spend their time with fewer, closer people, which Carstensen and colleagues (1999) linked to feeling that time is more limited, so that the most meaningful relationships matter more. People find new love at seventy and eighty, and people lose great loves and carry them always. A widower of seventy-eight meets a woman at his walking group, and when his children are surprised he tells them, “I loved your mother for fifty years. I still do. And I’m allowed to be happy now.”

    If it feels right, ask someone from another generation about love in their life. Older relatives usually have stories nobody has asked for.

    Dig deeper: love across the lifespan

  8. Love is something you do.

    Feelings of love come and go, while the actions of love can be steady. They include turning towards someone when they speak, keeping small promises, saying thank you and sorry, and making room for who they are. Physical closeness, like a hug or holding hands, matters a lot to some people and less to others, and sex is part of closeness in some relationships and not in others. What matters is that both people feel comfortable and free to say yes or no. Love never includes fear, threats or control.

    A woman notices that her friend has gone quiet since his divorce. She has never once said she loves him. Every Thursday she texts the single word “Walk?” and turns up at his door at six, in her old wax jacket, whatever the weather. Ask someone you love what small thing makes them feel cared for, and do it this week.

    Dig deeper: love as action

Your part, and only your part. You can share a little of yourself, listen well, turn towards the people you love and keep small promises. You can’t make someone love you, or love you in the way you want. If closeness keeps hurting you, or you feel afraid, that is not a failure of love on your part. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety)

The next Friday, 10:30pm

This time you leave both phones on the kitchen counter, make two cups of tea and ask Charlie what they’ve been thinking about lately that they haven’t told you. Charlie is quiet for a moment and then talks about their dad getting older, and how they dread the phone ringing late at night. You listen, and then you talk about the restructure at work. The tea goes cold, and it is midnight before either of you looks at the clock.

If you’re a teenager

First love can be huge and real, and so can a first breakup. Ines is sixteen when she is dumped by message on a Tuesday night, and she cries until two in the morning. Being told by adults that she will get over it doesn’t help. Telling her cousin, who simply listens, does, along with muting the chat instead of rereading it and a rule of no checking his profile after ten. A few weeks later she notices that a whole day has gone by without her thinking about him.

You could say “I don’t need advice, I just need to tell someone.” “Can we reply when we can, rather than all day?” And if you are the one ending it, “I don’t want to go out any more. I’m sorry. It isn’t about something you did wrong.”

Dig deeper: more worked examples

In everyday life

On your own

Being single, widowed, divorced or happily alone doesn’t mean a life without love, because friendships, family, community and the way you treat yourself are all places where love lives. If you want a partner and don’t have one, that longing is real and worth being gentle with (see On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own). Most partners drift into talking only about jobs and bills, and one real question a week can bring them back. Friendship needs tending like any other love, and families often love each other deeply and say it rarely, so a short “I’m glad you’re my sister” can mean a great deal.

  • Different levels of desire. This is very common in long relationships and is nobody’s fault. Talk at a calm time, keep some affection that doesn’t have to lead anywhere, and remember that a kind “no” is a no to the moment and never a rejection of the person. A qualified sex therapist or couples therapist can help. More in the full chapter (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-15-love-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

The spark fading doesn’t mean love is over; early intensity usually settles, and many long relationships stay warm and close and lively for decades. Nobody reads minds, either, however much they love you, so saying what helps is a gift and not a failure of romance.

  • “Jealousy proves love.” Feeling jealous is human, and asking for something out of care for the relationship is not control. Checking up without agreement, cutting someone off or punishing them is not love. See signs to look out for (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety#signs).

If you want to help someone else with this

Respect their kind of love, without assuming that everyone wants a partner or children. Be a safe person to tell things to, which means listening without judging and keeping what they share private. After a loss or a breakup, keep showing up, because many people get plenty of support for two weeks and very little after that.

  • If you’re worried about someone’s relationship, stay close and kind rather than criticising their partner. If they seem afraid, gently share Not safe at home?

Words you could use “I’m always glad to hear from you.” “You don’t have to explain your relationship to me. I just want you to be happy and safe.”

When to get more help

  • If you feel very lonely or low most days for two weeks or more, talk to a doctor or counsellor.
  • If closeness feels frightening, or you keep ending up in relationships that hurt you, a counsellor or therapist can help you understand why.
  • Couples or family counselling can help when you feel stuck, or keep having the same fight.
  • If someone you love controls you, frightens you, checks your phone, cuts you off from friends or pressures you into anything you don’t want, that isn’t love. Not safe at home? lists free, private help.
  • If you’re in danger now, call your local emergency number. Upset right now? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/upset-right-now) can help you take the first step.

This chapter is general education, not therapy.

Part Three · Chapter 16

Worry, low mood and trauma

How worry and anxiety work, the difference between a low patch and depression, what trauma is and isn’t, what helps day to day, how to support someone, and when and where to get more help. For anyone, in any kind of relationship, or on your own.

In this chapter

  1. Worry and anxiety are the body’s alarm
  2. Avoiding keeps fear going
  3. Give worry a time and a place
  4. Low mood is common. Depression is more than a bad week
  5. Doing often comes before feeling better
  6. Sleep, moving and people do a lot of the work
  7. Trauma is about what happened, and what it left behind
  8. After something frightening: safety, choice and no pressure
  9. Talking therapies help many people, and medicines can too
  10. If you’re a teenager
  11. In everyday life
  12. Common mix-ups
  13. If you want to help someone else with this
  14. When to get more help
  15. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  16. More for your situation

In short

  • Worry, low mood and the after-effects of trauma are common, human and treatable. They are not weakness, and they are not your fault.
  • They all run through the stress system from Chapter 2 (page 30). Small, steady things that settle the body and reconnect you with life help more than big pushes.
  • Avoiding and withdrawing feel safer but keep things going. Small steps back in, a little at a time, help most.
  • Talking therapies work for many people, and so can medicines. If it has lasted weeks, is getting in the way of life, or you feel unsafe, get help. If you might act on thoughts of ending your life, call or text 988 (US) or call Samaritans on 116 123 (UK and Ireland) now.

Sunday, 10:50pm

The house is quiet. You’ve checked the front door twice and the back door once. Tomorrow is the hospital appointment, ten o’clock, and the same three thoughts keep going round: what if it’s bad, what if you can’t cope, what if there’s nobody to tell. Your chest is tight and your mind won’t stop. And if you’re honest, you haven’t really wanted to see anyone for a few weeks now. Even answering messages has started to feel like too much.

Almost everyone worries, feels low or goes through something frightening at some point. For some people the feelings settle by themselves. For others they stick, and grow, until they shape every day. This chapter explains how they work, what tends to help, and when it’s time to ask for more. It can’t diagnose anyone. If any of this is about you right now, you aren’t alone, and things can get better.

Some tools elsewhere in the books lean on this chapter. The daily check-in’s “low, medium or high” (Part Two, Chapter I, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-1) lets the people around you adjust when worry or low mood has shrunk the room you have. “A full tank means later, not never” (Part Two, Chapter III, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-3) names a time to come back, because avoiding a thing keeps fear going. And picking one small goal (Part One, Next, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/self-3-next) suits low mood, since doing very often comes before feeling better.

  1. Worry and anxiety are the body’s alarm.

    Fear is the body’s alarm for danger that is here now. Anxiety is the same alarm ringing about something that might happen, and worry is the thinking part, the “What if…?” on repeat. All three run through the stress system described in Chapter 2 (page 30): a racing heart, a tight chest, shallow breathing, a churning stomach, poor sleep. The alarm is trying to protect you. The trouble is that it can be set too sensitive, and it can’t tell a real tiger from a worrying email.

    A fifteen-year-old’s heart pounds before every presentation in class. Nothing bad has ever happened in one. Her alarm still treats a room of her own classmates, half of whom she’s known since primary school, as a dangerous place. When worry rises, breathe out slowly five times, each out-breath longer than the in-breath, then name three things you can see. It tells the body that the danger isn’t here right now.

    Things to tell yourself “This is my alarm talking, and alarms can be wrong.” “My body is getting ready to protect me. I can thank it and carry on.”

    Dig deeper: how anxiety works

  2. Avoiding keeps fear going.

    When something makes us anxious, stepping away brings quick relief, and the relief teaches the brain that escaping was a good idea. So next time the fear is a little bigger and the world a little smaller. What helps is going back towards the feared thing in small, chosen steps, and staying long enough to learn that you can cope. Therapists call this exposure. Craske and colleagues (2014) describe how it works best when each step tests what you expect to happen.

    After a panic attack on the number 42, a man starts walking everywhere, even in the rain, even the three miles to work. With his sister beside him he rides one stop, then two. Some weeks later he does the whole journey into town, and his brain has slowly learned that buses are survivable. Pick one small thing you’ve been avoiding, break it into three steps from easiest to hardest, and do the easiest one this week.

    Things to tell yourself “What do I think will happen? Let’s see what actually happens.” “Uncomfortable isn’t the same as dangerous.”

    Dig deeper: avoidance and small steps
  3. zqaxunderstandingx16xworryxxworryxtimeqz

    Give worry a time and a place.

    Trying hard not to worry rarely works. What helps a lot of people is postponing it: you notice a worry, write it down, and save it for a set “worry time” later in the day. In an early study by Borkovec and colleagues (1983), people who practised this for four weeks reported worrying less each day. In worry time, ask of each worry whether there’s something you can do about it. If there is, plan one step. If there isn’t, practise letting it go.

    A man caring for his own father keeps a worry notebook by the kettle, a small red one. At six in the evening he gives it fifteen minutes with a cup of tea, and by then many of the morning’s worries already look smaller, and a couple have sorted themselves out. Choose a fifteen-minute worry time well before bed.

    Thoughts you could try “Noted. I’ll think about that at six.” “Can I do anything about this today? If not, it can wait.”

    Dig deeper: worry time and problem-solving

  4. Low mood is common. Depression is more than a bad week.

    Everyone has low days, and sadness after a loss or a disappointment is normal. Depression is different. It means low mood, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy, for most of the day, nearly every day, for two weeks or more, often with poor sleep, tiredness, changes in appetite, feeling worthless or guilty, and finding it hard to think. It can look like sadness. It can also look like irritability, or simply running on empty. It is a health problem, and nobody gets it by being weak.

    A retired teacher notices he has stopped going to his Thursday walking group, isn’t reading, and wakes at four every morning. He tells himself he’s just getting old, until his daughter, on a visit, gently suggests it might be depression and that depression can be treated. If you’ve felt low or lost interest most days for two weeks or more, book a talk with a doctor this week, and write down what you’ve noticed to take with you.

    You could say “I’ve not been myself for a few weeks, and I don’t think it’s just tiredness.” “I don’t enjoy things I used to. Can I talk to you about it?”

    Dig deeper: low mood and depression

  5. Doing often comes before feeling better.

    Low mood tells you to wait until you feel like it. Withdrawing makes life emptier, though, and that deepens the low. A well-tested approach called behavioural activation turns this round: you plan small, doable things that bring a bit of pleasure or a sense of having done something, and you do them whether you feel like it or not. A review of 26 trials by Ekers and colleagues (2014) found it helped with depression, though many of the studies were small.

    A woman living alone after her divorce plans three small things a day: a ten-minute walk to the postbox and back, one call or message, and one job she can finish, like wiping the hob. Some days they feel pointless. She does them anyway. Over a few weeks the days begin to feel less flat, though she couldn’t tell you which day it changed. Tomorrow, try three tiny things of your own, one for pleasure, one for connection and one you can finish.

    Things to tell yourself “I don’t have to feel like it to do it.” “Small counts.”

    Dig deeper: behavioural activation

  6. Sleep, moving and people do a lot of the work.

    These sound too simple to matter. The evidence for them is solid. Improving sleep can lift mood: in a large trial with university students, Freeman and colleagues (2017) found that an online sleep course reduced insomnia, and with it some other mental health difficulties.

    Exercise helps depression too. A review of 218 trials by Noetel and colleagues (2024) found walking or jogging, yoga and strength training all helped. Belonging to groups protects as well. Cruwys and colleagues (2013) found that people with depression who joined groups were less likely to relapse. A new dad who is exhausted and flat agrees with his partner on one protected long sleep each at the weekend, a pram walk every morning, and his old Wednesday five-a-side. Pick whichever of the three is most off for you right now and make one small change to it.

    Words you could use “I need help protecting my sleep for a while.” “Would you come for a short walk with me? I find it hard to go on my own.”

    Dig deeper: sleep, exercise and connection

    Professor Puddles

    Small, steady things help: a walk, a regular bedtime, time with someone kind. Calm sounds can be a soft way to wind down at night.

    Tool: Cool-down corner: calm sounds and music spreadloveandacceptance.com/soundscapes

  7. Trauma is about what happened, and what it left behind.

    Trauma usually means going through, or seeing, something that threatened life or safety, such as violence, abuse, a serious accident, war, or the sudden death of someone close. It is very common. In surveys across 24 countries, Kessler and colleagues (2017) found about 7 in 10 adults had been through at least one.

    Most people recover over time. A smaller number develop post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), with memories that come back vividly, avoiding reminders, feeling on high alert, and sleep problems. Ordinary hard times and stress hurt too, even when they aren’t trauma in this sense.

    Months after a car crash on a wet roundabout, a woman still jumps at screeching brakes and won’t drive after dark. Her alarm learned that cars can mean danger and hasn’t yet unlearned it, which is a long way from overreacting. If something frightening happened more than a month ago and it still shapes your days, talk to a doctor. Trauma-focused talking therapies help many people.

    Things to tell yourself “My reactions make sense after what happened.” “It’s in the past, even if my body doesn’t feel that yet.”

    Dig deeper: what trauma is and isn’t

  8. After something frightening: safety, choice and no pressure.

    After a frightening event, people need safety, practical help, warmth and choice. They don’t need to be made to talk. A review of single-session “debriefing” after trauma by Rose and colleagues (2002) found it did not prevent PTSD, and might make things worse for some. Services that are “trauma-informed” (SAMHSA, 2014) put safety, trust, choice and working together first, and the same ideas help in families, friendships and workplaces.

    After a break-in, a grandmother doesn’t want to talk about it. Her grandson doesn’t push. He fixes the back-door lock, stays the night on her sofa, and says, “If you ever want to talk about it, I’m here.” A week later, over the phone, she does.

    Ways to say it “You don’t have to tell me anything. What would help right now?” “You’re safe now. I’m staying.”

    Dig deeper: trauma-informed care

  9. Talking therapies help many people, and medicines can too.

    Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) teaches practical ways to notice and change patterns of thinking and doing. It’s one of the most studied talking therapies, and a review of over a hundred meta-analyses by Hofmann and colleagues (2012) found the strongest support for anxiety problems and stress, and support for many other problems too.

    Guidelines such as NICE (2022) also recommend guided self-help, behavioural activation, exercise groups and, for some people, antidepressants. Questions about medicine, including starting, changing or stopping it, are for a doctor or prescriber. Please don’t stop a medicine suddenly without advice.

    A young man is too embarrassed to ask for help with panic attacks, until one stops him getting on the 7.40 for the second week running. His GP refers him to a short course of CBT, and after eight sessions he’s taking the train to work again, with a book and a bottle of water for the bad days. Before an appointment, it helps to write three lines: what you’ve noticed, how long it has lasted, and what it’s stopping you doing.

    Words to try “I’d like to talk about my mood. It’s been going on for a while.” “What are my options, and what do you recommend for someone like me?”

    Dig deeper: what treatment involves

Your part, and only your part. You can learn how your alarm works, keep the basics going, take small steps back towards life, and ask for help when it’s more than you can carry. You can’t think your way out of depression by trying harder, and you can’t fix someone else’s. Being kind to yourself, and getting the right help, are part of the work. If you feel unsafe, reaching out today matters more than anything in this book.

Monday, 7:30am

Last night you wrote the three worries on the back of an envelope from the gas board and told them they could wait until today, and you slept a little. This morning you breathe out long at the kitchen window, then text your neighbour: “Hospital at ten. A bit scared. Fancy a cuppa after?”

She replies with three hearts and says of course. The appointment is still the appointment. You won’t be facing it on your own, though. Looking at the envelope again, you notice how many weeks it’s been since you felt like yourself, and you add one more line at the bottom, to ask the doctor about your mood as well.

If you’re a teenager

Exams, friends, group chats and the future can all pile up at once, usually at about one in the morning. Tolu is seventeen and can’t sleep the night before a chemistry exam. She writes the worry down for tomorrow’s ten-minute worry time, plans one small step (ask Mr Okafor about question types) and puts her phone on the landing. The next day she tells her mum, and it helps more than she expected it to.

If worry or low mood is stopping you sleeping or going to school most days for a few weeks, tell someone you trust or your doctor. Under 19 in the UK, you can call Childline free on 0800 1111.

You could say “I keep worrying at night. Can I talk it through?” “I don’t need you to fix it. I just need to say it.”

Dig deeper: give worry a time and a place

In everyday life

Living alone can make worry louder at night and low mood quieter and easier to miss, so one small contact a day is worth protecting, even a two-minute call (see On your own: when it’s lonely, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own). With a partner, low mood can look like not caring and anxiety can look like nagging, so name it plainly: “I’m low today, and I’m not cross with you.” Children and teenagers get anxious and low too, and calm, routine and listening help them more than reassurance on repeat. A friend who keeps cancelling may be struggling. Keep inviting them, with no pressure to say yes.

Grief and depression overlap without being the same thing, and Chapter 8 (page 112) looks at grief on its own terms. At work, a short, honest line to a manager often opens up more support than people expect. If you have ADHD, avoidance often looks like putting things off, so make the first step almost silly (“open the envelope”), set a ten-minute timer, or do it with someone else in the room. More in the full chapter (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-16-worry-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

Anxiety doesn’t mean something is wrong with you. It’s a normal alarm, and it only becomes a problem when it rings too loud or too often, or starts shrinking your life. Depression isn’t just sadness, and nobody snaps out of it; it affects sleep, energy, thinking and the body as well as mood, and many people recover with the right help. Not everything bad that happens is trauma in the clinical sense, which usually means a threat to life or safety, but other hard things still hurt and still deserve care, and the word doesn’t need to fit for help to be fair. Talking about trauma straight away doesn’t help everyone. Some people want to and some don’t, forcing it can make things worse, and safety and choice come first.

And asking someone about suicide does not put the idea in their head. A review by Dazzi and colleagues (2014) found no evidence that asking increases suicidal thoughts, and it may help.

If you want to help someone else with this

Notice, and ask. “You’ve seemed low lately. How are you doing, really?” opens the door, and after that it helps to listen more than you talk. Leave the feeling alone rather than arguing with it; “Cheer up” and “It could be worse” push people away, while “That sounds really hard” keeps them close. Offer something specific, like a walk, a meal, a lift to the doctor or an evening on the sofa together, because a small practical offer is much easier to accept than a big vague one.

Ask directly about safety if you’re worried. “Are you having thoughts of ending your life?” If yes, stay with them, and get help together today. And look after yourself too, because supporting someone who is struggling is tiring (see Chapter 12, page 170).

Words you could use “I’m not trying to fix it. I just want you to know I’m here.” “Would it help if I came with you to the doctor?”

zqaxunderstandingx16xworryxxmorexhelpqzWhen to get more help

Talk to a doctor, a counsellor or a mental health service if:

  • you’ve felt low, empty or hopeless, or lost interest in things, most days for two weeks or more;
  • worry or panic is stopping you doing things, or you’re avoiding more and more;
  • something frightening happened over a month ago and still shapes your days and nights;
  • you’re using alcohol, drugs, food or anything else to cope;
  • you’re not sleeping, eating or looking after yourself;
  • you have thoughts of harming yourself.

If you might act on thoughts of ending your life, or you are in danger, get help now. Call your local emergency number (911 in the US and Canada, 999 in the UK, 112 in most of Europe). In the US, call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or text HOME to 741741. In the UK and Ireland, call Samaritans free on 116 123, or text SHOUT to 85258.

In Canada, call or text 988. In Australia, call Lifeline on 13 11 14. In New Zealand, call or text 1737. Under 19 in the UK? Childline is free on 0800 1111. Anywhere else, findahelpline.com lists free helplines in your country. More are on Someone to talk to, free (spreadloveandacceptance.com/outside-help).

In England you can usually refer yourself to NHS Talking Therapies without seeing a GP first. Find a counsellor or therapist (spreadloveandacceptance.com/outside-help#counsellor) has more places to start. If someone at home is hurting or frightening you, Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private help.

This chapter is general education. It isn’t a diagnosis or a substitute for care from a professional.
